chapter_title: Analysis of Settlement and Volume Expansion

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.summary: Introduces Chapter 5 on analysis of settlement and volume expansion in soil. Covers the scope of volume change processes including compression-induced settlement and swelling-induced heave, identifies the three primary settlement mechanisms, and distinguishes behavior between fine-grained and coarse-grained soils. Sets the stage for methods and criteria discussed throughout the chapter.
key_points: Chapter covers both settlement (compression) and heave (expansion) of soils under changed conditions.
Three primary settlement mechanisms: immediate distortion, consolidation, and secondary compression.
Fine-grained soils allow separation of settlement components due to low hydraulic conductivity and high compressibility.
Coarse-grained soils consolidate quickly, making separation from immediate deformation difficult.
Special cases such as collapsing soils are covered in DM 7.2 (UFC 3-220-20).
sections.applicability: Applies as an overview section to all analyses of soil volume change, settlement, and heave addressed in Chapter 5.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Defines the scope of Chapter 5, covering practical aspects of soil volume change including settlement from engineered fill placement, foundation loading, and groundwater lowering, as well as volume expansion (heave) in swelling soils. Both immediate and long-term settlement are addressed, including tolerable settlement criteria, rate of settlement, and methods to reduce or accelerate settlement.
sections.body:
This chapter explains the practical aspects of the process of volume change in soil. Many of the cases relate to the compression of soil layers due to changed conditions, such as placement of an engineered fill, foundation loading, or lowering of the groundwater table. Compression of soil results in settlement, which is vertical displacement of the ground surface or a structure supported by the ground. Both immediate and long-term settlement will be considered, along with tolerable settlement criteria, the rate of settlement, and methods to reduce or accelerate settlement. Swelling soils can also change volume by expansion, which is often referred to as heave.

Guidance on special cases, such as collapsing soils, is provided in DM 7.2 (UFC 3-220-20). Chapter 2 of this document provides guidance on methods for monitoring settlement.
key_points: Scope includes compression from engineered fill, foundation loads, and groundwater table lowering.
Settlement defined as vertical displacement of ground surface or a supported structure.
Both immediate and long-term settlement are covered, including tolerable limits and acceleration/reduction methods.
Heave (volume expansion) in swelling soils is also within scope.
Special cases (e.g., collapsing soils) are deferred to DM 7.2 (UFC 3-220-20).
Chapter 2 covers field methods for monitoring settlement.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the scope of analyses covered in Chapter 5 for any project involving soil volume change, settlement, or heave.

sections.title: Occurrence of Settlement
sections.summary: Describes the three primary mechanisms of settlement—immediate distortion, consolidation, and secondary compression—and explains how their relative contributions differ between fine-grained and coarse-grained soils. Highlights that fine-grained soils allow separation of mechanisms due to low hydraulic conductivity, while coarse-grained soils consolidate rapidly. References Table 5-1 for a summary of settlement processes and calculation methods by soil type.
sections.body:
Settlement is the result of three primary mechanisms: (1) immediate distortion that occurs in response to the application of a new load, (2) consolidation, which is compression of the soil skeleton in response to changes in effective stress, and (3) secondary compression, which is rearrangement of the soil structure under constant effective stress. All three mechanisms will be explained in more detail in later sections of this chapter.

In saturated fine-grained soils, the settlement associated with the three mechanisms can be distinguished and separated for the practical purpose of estimating settlement magnitude. This separation is possible because these soils have low hydraulic conductivity and relatively high compressibility, which causes consolidation to occur over a measurable period of time. The processes and magnitudes of settlement typically associated with fine-grained soils are summarized in Table 5-1.

Coarse-grained soils are much less compressible than fine-grained soils and have higher hydraulic conductivity. Because of these characteristics, consolidation occurs very quickly and can be difficult to separate from immediate deformation. Much of the compression of coarse-grained soil is related to particle rearrangement under changed stress. Vibrations from earthquakes, blasting, or machinery can also cause settlement of coarse-grained soil. Submergence and soaking of coarse-grained soils, particularly fill materials, can lead to settlement as discussed in Section 5-9.
key_points: Three settlement mechanisms: (1) immediate distortion, (2) consolidation (effective stress change), (3) secondary compression (constant effective stress).
Fine-grained soils: low hydraulic conductivity allows measurable, separable consolidation over time.
Coarse-grained soils: consolidation is rapid and hard to distinguish from immediate deformation.
Particle rearrangement under changed stress dominates compression in coarse-grained soils.
Vibrations (earthquakes, blasting, machinery) and submergence/soaking can also cause settlement in coarse-grained soils.
Table 5-1 summarizes settlement processes and calculation methods by soil type.
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying and distinguishing settlement mechanisms for any soil type subjected to new loading or changed stress conditions.

sections.title: Occurrence of Heave
sections.summary: Describes the mechanisms causing soil heave (volume expansion), including reduction of total vertical stress (from excavation, erosion, or load removal) and reduction of matric suction (lowering effective stress and increasing void ratio). Discusses the role of soil mineralogy—especially expansive clays like montmorillonite and vermiculite—as well as ice lens formation and chemical reactions such as pyrite oxidation as additional causes of heave.
sections.body: Heave or swell occurs primarily due to the reduction of total vertical stress or the reduction of matric suction, which both lower the effective stress on the soil and therefore allow an increase in the void ratio. The reduction of total stress occurs as the result of excavation or erosion of soil, as well as the removal of man-made loading. The matric suction in a soil depends on the soil type and the past and present atmospheric conditions. Especially important is the degree of saturation of the soil. The factors affecting the degree of saturation include climate history, topography, vegetation, and groundwater level. The amount of swelling that occurs as a result of either mechanism depends on the size and type of minerals that comprise the soil. Clay minerals with very small particles and high specific surface area, such as montmorillonite and vermiculite, are most susceptible to swelling. Heave can also occur as a result of the formation of ice lenses in frozen soil. Volumetric expansion from chemical reactions, such as pyrite, can also cause heave.
key_points: Heave is driven by reduction of total vertical stress (excavation, erosion, load removal) or reduction of matric suction.
Both mechanisms lower effective stress, allowing an increase in void ratio and volume expansion.
Matric suction is influenced by climate history, topography, vegetation, and groundwater level.
Expansive clay minerals with high specific surface area (montmorillonite, vermiculite) are most susceptible to swelling.
Ice lens formation in frozen soils and chemical reactions (e.g., pyrite oxidation) are additional heave mechanisms.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating potential for upward volume expansion (heave) in soils subject to stress relief, moisture change, freeze-thaw, or reactive mineralogy.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.summary: Defines the conditions under which the settlement analysis methods in Chapter 5 are valid. Methods apply only when shear stresses are well below the shear strength of the soil. Consolidation magnitude, rate, and secondary compression analyses additionally assume the soil is saturated. Violation of these conditions requires alternative or supplemental approaches.
sections.body: The methods to analyze settlement that are presented in this chapter apply to conditions where shear stresses are well below the shear strength. In addition, these analyses of consolidation magnitude and rate as well as secondary compression assume that the soil is saturated.
key_points: Settlement methods in Chapter 5 are valid only when shear stresses are well below the shear strength.
Consolidation magnitude, rate, and secondary compression analyses assume fully saturated soil conditions.
Unsaturated or near-failure conditions require methods outside the scope of this chapter.
sections.applicability: Applies when verifying that site conditions (stress state and saturation) fall within the assumptions required for the settlement analysis methods presented in Chapter 5.

sections.title: Mechanics of Consolidation
sections.summary: Container section covering the fundamental mechanics of soil consolidation, including the consolidation process, initial stress states, stress history, evaluation of existing conditions, and change in vertical stress. Provides the conceptual and analytical framework needed to estimate both the magnitude and rate of consolidation settlement.
key_points: Consolidation is driven by changes in effective stress resulting from dissipation of excess pore water pressure over time.
Both magnitude and rate of consolidation must be evaluated; each requires different input parameters.
Stress history (NC vs. OC vs. underconsolidated) fundamentally controls soil behavior under new loading.
Existing conditions at the start of construction must be evaluated before applying new stress changes.
sections.applicability: Applies as an overarching framework whenever consolidation settlement analysis is required for a saturated soil mass.

sections.title: Consolidation Process
sections.summary: Explains the physical mechanism of consolidation: when total stress increases abruptly in saturated soil, excess pore water pressure (ux) develops instantly equal to Δσz, then dissipates over time as water drains, transferring stress to the soil skeleton. Covers what is needed to estimate both magnitude and rate of consolidation settlement.
sections.body:
Consolidation of soil is caused by changes in effective stress. For this reason, it is necessary to consider the process by which effective stresses change within a soil mass. Saturated soil consists of two relatively incompressible components, the mineral particles and water. In comparison, the overall soil structure is compressible because the particles can rearrange to encompass more or less void space. The compressible soil structure must strain or deform in order to support a change in stress.

When a soil mass experiences an abrupt change in the applied total normal stress, the soil must respond in one of two ways: (1) the compressible soil structure strains instantaneously, or (2) a pressure change occurs in the incompressible water within the soil voids. The first option is not possible because strain of the soil structure requires a change in the void ratio of the soil. The void ratio of a saturated soil can only change if the amount of water in the soil changes, and time is required for water to leave or enter the soil voids. Instead, the instantaneous soil response follows the second option, and a change in the pore water pressure occurs. This temporarily altered pressure is often referred to as excess pore water pressure, ux. For saturated, one-dimensional conditions, the magnitude of ux will be roughly equal to the change in total vertical stress, Δσz. Because Δσz is balanced by ux, the instantaneous change in effective stress is negligible, and there is no instantaneous settlement as a result of consolidation.

The excess pore water pressure in the soil creates a hydraulic gradient between the conditions within the soil and those at its boundaries. The gradient causes water to flow out of or into the soil, as time progresses following the application of Δσz. When Δσz is positive, the soil volume decreases as the water flows out and the excess pore water pressures decrease. After a relatively long period of time, the excess pore water pressure dissipates completely (i.e., ux = 0), all of the change in total vertical stress is transferred to the soil structure, and the consolidation settlement is complete. The time required to reach this state can range from seconds or minutes for thin layers of coarse-grained soils to years for thick layers of fine-grained soil.

Estimates of the magnitude of consolidation require (1) knowledge of the initial vertical stress state, (2) prediction of the change in total stress caused by new loading, (3) an understanding of the stress history of the soils impacted by the changes, and (4) knowledge of the compressibility characteristics of those soils.

Estimates of the rate of consolidation settlement require knowledge of (1) the hydraulic boundary conditions, (2) the thickness, (3) the compressibility, and (4) the hydraulic conductivity of the compressible soil layers.
key_points: Saturated soil is nearly incompressible instantaneously; an abrupt load increase generates excess pore water pressure ux ≈ Δσz rather than immediate settlement.
Consolidation settlement occurs as water drains over time, ux dissipates, and effective stress increases to equal the applied total stress change.
Time to complete consolidation ranges from seconds (thin coarse-grained layers) to years (thick fine-grained layers).
Magnitude of consolidation requires: initial stress state, stress change, stress history, and compressibility characteristics.
Rate of consolidation requires: hydraulic boundary conditions, layer thickness, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a saturated soil mass is subjected to a change in total normal stress and consolidation settlement must be assessed.

sections.title: Initial Vertical Stress State
sections.summary: Describes how to establish the initial geostatic vertical total stress (σz0), pore water pressure (u0), and vertical effective stress (σ′z0) prior to consolidation analysis. Distinguishes hydrostatic from artesian pore water pressure conditions and their effects on effective stress calculation, referencing Figure 5-1.
sections.body:
Consolidation analysis focuses on volume change caused by changes in vertical stress. The initial geostatic vertical total stress (σz0), pore water pressure (u0), and vertical effective stress (σʹz0) should be calculated using methods discussed in Chapter 4. Figure 5-1(a) illustrates initial vertical stress conditions for hydrostatic water conditions.

Artesian water conditions are associated with confined aquifers in which higher pore water pressure is present in a more permeable soil layer below a confining stratum. Artesian conditions affect the calculation of pore water pressure within the compressible layer as well as the calculated vertical effective stress. As illustrated in Figure 5-1(b), the hydrostatic pore water pressure is labeled u0 while the artesian pressure at any depth is Δu. The artesian pressure must also be subtracted from the total vertical stress in order to obtain the correct initial effective stress.
key_points: Initial stresses σz0, u0, and σ′z0 must be established before any consolidation calculation using Chapter 4 methods.
Hydrostatic conditions are the standard case; artesian conditions require additional correction to pore pressure and effective stress.
Under artesian conditions, excess artesian pressure Δu must be subtracted from total vertical stress to obtain correct σ′z0.
Figure 5-1 illustrates both hydrostatic and artesian initial vertical stress profiles.
sections.applicability: Applies at the start of any consolidation analysis where the initial vertical stress state must be defined, including sites with artesian groundwater conditions.

sections.title: Stress History
sections.summary: Defines stress history concepts critical to consolidation analysis: preconsolidation stress σ′p, normally consolidated (NC), overconsolidated (OC), and underconsolidated states. Introduces the overconsolidation ratio (OCR = σ′p/σ′z0) and illustrates in-situ stress profiles for steady-state and transient conditions via Figures 5-2 and 5-3.
sections.body:
The stress history of a soil refers to the past stress states that the soil has experienced. It will affect the structure and behavior of the soil under new loading. This is especially true for fine-grained soils. Of particular importance is the highest vertical effective stress to which the soil has been consolidated, which is known as the preconsolidation stress or maximum past pressure, σʹp. A method for determining the preconsolidation stress is shown in Figure 3-12.

For some soil deposits, the existing vertical effective stress is the highest vertical effective stress the soil has ever experienced and σʹp is equal to σʹz0. This type of soil deposit is referred to as normally consolidated and sometimes abbreviated "NC."

More commonly, soil deposits have been preloaded or preconsolidated at some point in the past, and σʹz0 is less than σʹp. This type of soil is referred to as overconsolidated and sometimes abbreviated "OC." The overconsolidation ratio (OCR) is a helpful measure of soil behavior and is found as:

OCR = σʹp / σʹz0

where:
σʹp = preconsolidation stress and
σʹz0 = current vertical effective stress.

In situ vertical stress profiles for steady state conditions are summarized in Figure 5-2. In Figure 5-2(a), the clay layer is normally consolidated because the preconsolidation stress is equal to the effective vertical stress. The clay in Figure 5-2(b) is slightly overconsolidated as a result of a higher groundwater level compared to (a), which reduces the current vertical effective stress. Similarly, overconsolidation as a result of excavation (or erosion) and previous loading are depicted in Figure 5-2(c) and (d).

In some cases, a soil layer may be encountered that has not yet finished consolidating as a result of a prior change in effective stress. This state is referred to as underconsolidated. In this case, the pore water pressures in the soil have not yet reached equilibrium following a change in stress and are higher than the hydrostatic values. Two examples are provided in Figure 5-3. In the first example, the groundwater level has been lowered in the sand layers. The decrease in pore pressure (and corresponding consolidation) of the low permeability clay layer will be time-dependent. The second example is partial consolidation under a prior applied stress. In either case, the initial pore pressure variation with depth within the clay layer must be measured or estimated in order to calculate the variation of initial vertical effective stress within the soil.
key_points: Preconsolidation stress σ′p is the maximum past vertical effective stress; it governs whether the soil responds stiffly (OC) or compressibly (NC) to new loads.
OCR = σ′p / σ′z0; OCR = 1 for normally consolidated soils, OCR > 1 for overconsolidated soils.
Sources of overconsolidation include glaciation, erosion, excavation, prior loading, and groundwater fluctuations.
Underconsolidated soils have pore pressures above hydrostatic equilibrium, meaning consolidation from a prior event is still ongoing.
For underconsolidated soils, in-situ pore pressure profiles must be measured or estimated to establish initial effective stresses correctly.

equations.description: Overconsolidation ratio: OCR = σ′p / σ′z0, where σ′p is the preconsolidation stress and σ′z0 is the current vertical effective stress.

sections.applicability: Applies whenever consolidation settlement analysis requires characterization of soil stress history, particularly for fine-grained soils subject to overconsolidation or underconsolidation.

sections.title: Evaluation of Existing Conditions
sections.summary: Outlines the step-by-step evaluation of existing site conditions required before settlement calculations. Steps include reviewing site/geologic data, determining preconsolidation stress from lab tests or undrained strength correlations (Eq. 5-2 and 5-3), comparing σ′p to σ′z0, and identifying underconsolidation through pore pressure measurements. References Figure 5-4.
sections.body:
For purposes of settlement calculations, the existing conditions at the start of construction or the application of a new load must be evaluated. At a minimum, this evaluation should include the following steps:

• Review the available site and geologic data. In particular, determine potential sources of overconsolidation (e.g., glaciation, erosion, human activity, groundwater fluctuations) and estimate the likely magnitude of preconsolidation and/or OCR.

• Determine the variation of the preconsolidation stress with depth from laboratory consolidation tests (see Chapter 3). Measurements of undrained shear strength can also be used along with correlations to provide additional estimates of preconsolidation stress. For example, undrained strength (su) is often related to the in situ vertical stress and the OCR by:

su ≈ USRNC · σ′z0 · OCR^m

where:
USRNC = the soil's normally consolidated undrained strength ratio, and
m = an empirical coefficient (See Section 8-3).

Equation 5-2 can be rearranged to obtain:

σ′p ≈ σ′z0 · (su / (USRNC · σ′z0))^(1/m)

• Compare estimates of preconsolidation stress to current vertical effective stress. A helpful tool for this purpose is a plot showing the subsurface profile, the laboratory test data, and the variation of effective vertical stress with depth, such as that shown in Figure 5-4.

• If underconsolidation is expected or indicated, measurements of pore water pressure with depth are required to identify the extent of the underconsolidation.
key_points: Site and geologic data review is the first step; identify potential overconsolidation sources such as glaciation, erosion, prior loading, or groundwater changes.
Preconsolidation stress should be determined from lab consolidation tests; undrained strength measurements provide a secondary estimate via Eq. 5-2.
Eq. 5-2: su ≈ USRNC · σ′z0 · OCR^m; can be rearranged (Eq. 5-3) to back-calculate σ′p from measured su.
Plot σ′p and σ′z0 versus depth (as in Figure 5-4) to visually assess consolidation state throughout the profile.
Pore pressure measurements with depth are mandatory when underconsolidation is suspected.

equations.description: Undrained strength correlation: su ≈ USRNC · σ′z0 · OCR^m, where USRNC is the normally consolidated undrained strength ratio and m is an empirical coefficient.
Rearranged form of Eq. 5-2 to estimate preconsolidation stress: σ′p ≈ σ′z0 · (su / (USRNC · σ′z0))^(1/m).

sections.applicability: Applies before any settlement calculation is performed, specifically to characterize existing stress conditions and consolidation state at the start of construction or load application.

sections.title: Change in Vertical Stress
sections.summary: Directs the engineer to use Chapter 4 methods to compute Δσz at required depths within compressible layers. Notes that wide surcharge loads produce uniform Δσz, while most other loading conditions produce Δσz that varies with depth and lateral position, requiring the engineer to select critical settlement evaluation locations.
sections.body: The methods presented in Chapter 4 should be used to evaluate the change in vertical stress at the required depths within the compressible soil layer. Surcharge loads of wide lateral extent will result in constant value of Δσz. Most other loading conditions will result in Δσz that varies with both depth and lateral location below the applied load. It is the responsibility of the engineer to determine the critical locations at which settlement will be evaluated.
key_points: Δσz within the compressible layer must be evaluated using Chapter 4 stress distribution methods.
Wide surcharge loads produce approximately uniform Δσz throughout the compressible layer.
Most loads produce Δσz varying with both depth and lateral distance from the load; the engineer must select critical evaluation points.
Selection of critical settlement evaluation locations is an engineering judgment responsibility.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the change in vertical stress input needed for consolidation settlement calculations under any applied loading condition.

sections.title: Settlement Calculations
sections.summary: Top-level container section introducing the framework for settlement calculations in UFC 3-220-10. Covers the basic principle that settlement equals the sum of vertical strains across compressible soil layers, defines key geometric terms (B, L, q0), and introduces the two main approaches to defining soil layers for settlement analysis.
key_points: Settlement is the sum of vertical strains multiplied by layer thicknesses across all compressible soil layers beneath a load.
Foundation geometry is central to many settlement methods: B = shortest dimension, L = longest dimension, q0 = applied stress at foundation base.
Most settlement calculations separate into a vertical strain component and an initial layer thickness component.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever settlement calculations are being performed for any soil type using UFC 3-220-10 procedures.

sections.title: Basic Formulation
sections.summary: Defines the fundamental equation for settlement (Eq. 5-4): settlement s equals the sum of vertical strain εz,i times layer thickness Hi over all n compressible layers. Establishes that settlement equals the change in total thickness of underlying soil, and introduces notation for foundation geometry (B, L, q0) used throughout the chapter.
sections.body:
At the most basic level, settlement at the ground surface is equal to the change in thickness of the soil underlying a load. The change in thickness (∆H) divided by the initial thickness (H) is equal to the vertical strain (engineering strain). Thus, settlement (s) is the sum of the vertical strain (εz) caused by ∆σz for each compressible soil layer multiplied by the initial thickness of each layer, or:

s = ΣHi = Σεz,i · Hi  (5-4)

where: Hi = thickness of each layer in same units as s.

Most settlement calculations can be split into a component related to the vertical strain and a component related to the initial layer thickness. This concept can be used to understand the calculation procedures at a deeper level.

Many of the settlement prediction methods in this chapter use foundation geometry to define influence factors or to select the appropriate procedure. The shortest dimension of the foundation or loaded area will be designated as B while the longest dimension is L. The applied stress at the base of the foundation is indicated by q0.
key_points: Settlement s = Σ(εz,i × Hi), summing vertical strain times thickness for each compressible layer (Eq. 5-4).
Vertical strain εz is induced by the change in vertical stress ∆σz at each layer.
B = shortest foundation dimension, L = longest dimension, q0 = applied stress at foundation base — standard notation for this chapter.
Settlement calculations generally decompose into a strain component and a layer thickness component.

equations.description: Settlement s equals the summation of vertical strain εz,i multiplied by layer thickness Hi for each of n compressible soil layers: s = Σ(εz,i · Hi).

sections.applicability: Applies to all settlement calculations where the compressible profile is subdivided into discrete layers with assigned vertical strains.

sections.title: Soil Layers in Settlement Calculations
sections.summary: Describes three approaches to defining soil layers for settlement calculations. Distortion settlement of fine-grained soils and total settlement of coarse-grained soils often use a single layer with built-in influence factors. Consolidation settlement typically requires multiple layers of equal or increasing thickness with depth, balancing accuracy against computational effort. Soil properties must be constant within each defined layer.
sections.body:
Calculations of distortion settlement of fine-grained soils and total settlement of coarse-grained soils often treat the soil as one layer. In this case, the effect of the variation in strain with depth below the load is built into the calculation procedure and influence factors. This approach is illustrated by Figure 5-5(a).

In contrast, consolidation settlement of fine-grained soils is typically calculated by dividing the soil into multiple layers. The vertical strain is determined for each soil layer, which allows the effects of load geometry and changing soil conditions to be considered explicitly. Figure 5-5(b) shows a layer of compressible soil divided into many thin layers of equal thickness. This method is flexible and theoretically sound but requires a large number of calculations that may be tedious if not automated. Figure 5-5(c) illustrates an approach in which the layer thickness increases with depth. This method recognizes that conditions change most quickly near the load. Regardless of the method used to define soil layers, soil properties within a given layer should be constant. Actual layer boundaries in the subsurface profile must supersede the layer division suggestions in Figure 5-5.
key_points: Distortion settlement (fine-grained) and total settlement (coarse-grained) often treat the soil as a single layer; strain variation with depth is embedded in influence factors.
Consolidation settlement of fine-grained soils requires multiple layers so load geometry and varying soil conditions can be modeled explicitly.
Equal-thickness sublayers (Fig. 5-5b) are flexible and theoretically rigorous but computationally intensive without automation.
Increasing layer thickness with depth (Fig. 5-5c) reflects that stress and strain change most rapidly near the applied load.
Soil properties must be constant within each defined layer; actual subsurface layer boundaries override suggested layer divisions.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a soil layering scheme for any settlement calculation, particularly consolidation settlement of fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Settlement of Coarse-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Introduces the overall framework for calculating settlement in coarse-grained soils. Distortion and consolidation settlement occur rapidly, so components are often combined. Multiple calculation methods are available, most relying on CPT or SPT field test results due to the difficulty of sampling coarse-grained soils. Secondary compression is typically estimated as a proportion of short-term settlement.
sections.body: As indicated in Table 5-1, distortion and consolidation settlement occur in coarse-grained soils in a relatively short time span. If considered, secondary compression of these soils is typically estimated as a proportion of the calculated short-term settlement. For this reason, it is common practice to combine the components of settlement for coarse-grained soils. A variety of calculation methods are available. The soil properties for most of the methods are based on the results of field tests, such as CPT or SPT, due to the variability and difficulty of sampling coarse-grained soils.
key_points: Distortion and consolidation settlement in coarse-grained soils occur in a relatively short time span.
Secondary compression is typically estimated as a proportion of the calculated short-term settlement.
Settlement components for coarse-grained soils are commonly combined into a single calculation.
Most methods rely on CPT or SPT field test results due to the difficulty of obtaining undisturbed samples.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating total settlement of foundations on coarse-grained soils using any of the available calculation methods.

sections.title: Short Term Settlement of Coarse-Grained Soil
sections.summary: Container section covering three approaches to calculating short-term settlement of coarse-grained soils: the Elastic Method, the Schmertmann Method, and Empirical Methods. Also includes a subsection on accuracy and reliability of the various methods based on case history evaluations.
key_points: Short-term settlement methods for coarse-grained soils include elastic, Schmertmann, and empirical approaches.
Field test data (CPT, SPT) are the primary basis for soil property inputs across all methods.
Method selection should balance accuracy and reliability depending on project requirements.
sections.applicability: Applies when calculating short-term (immediate) settlement of foundations bearing on coarse-grained soils.

sections.title: Elastic Method
sections.summary: Presents the elastic settlement equation (Eq. 5-5) for coarse-grained soils modeled as an elastic medium, defining influence factors µ0 and µ1 from Figure 5-6. Discusses the role of the (1-ν²) term, appropriate H/B ratios (4–5B critical depth), and selection of Es from Table 5-2 using average SPT N60 values. Includes a correction formula (Eq. 5-6) for dense saturated silty sands.
sections.body:
If the soil supporting a load is idealized as an elastic medium with a modulus equal to Es and Poisson's ratio of ν, the resulting settlement (s) is:

s = q0 · B · µ0 · µ1 / Es  (Eq. 5-5)

where:
q0 = stress applied by load,
B = width of the applied load,
µ0 = influence factor associated with embedment of the load, and
µ1 = influence factor associated with the problem geometry and Poisson's ratio.

Some sources report Equation 5-5 with a (1-ν²) term. This term is often combined with the influence factors directly. When using charts and tables for µ1, the engineer must check carefully to determine whether or not the (1-ν²) term has been included and what value of ν has been assumed, if appropriate.

The influence factors, µ1 and µ0, can be found using Figure 5-6 for the ratios of L/B, H/B, and D/B represented by the problem geometry. Note that H/B ratios can theoretically be very high, when a significant depth of soil is present below a loaded area. However, based on the concept of critical depth (see Section 4-2.1.5), the zone that contributes to settlement typically has a thickness of 4B to 5B below the loaded area. The use of H/B ratios greater than 4 to 5 may overestimate settlement.

The settlement predicted by Equation 5-5 will be directly related to the value of Es, which is a difficult parameter to measure or obtain. General guidance for the selection of Es for coarse-grained soils is provided in Table 5-2. Most of the correlations summarized in this table are based on the results of Standard Penetration Test (SPT) blow counts. An average SPT value (Nʹ) is used to predict settlement in coarse-grained soils. In most cases, Nʹ is equal the average N60 value from the bottom of the loaded area to a depth of B below the load. In dense, saturated silty sands, the value of NʹSM is calculated as:

NʹSM = 15 + 0.5(Nʹ - 15)  (Eq. 5-6)

where:
Nʹ = average N60 value.
key_points: Elastic settlement is calculated as s = q0·B·µ0·µ1/Es (Eq. 5-5), where µ0 and µ1 are influence factors from Figure 5-6.
Some formulations include a (1-ν²) term combined into the influence factors; engineers must verify which convention a chart uses.
The effective settlement zone is typically 4B–5B below the loaded area; H/B ratios > 4–5 may overestimate settlement.
Es for coarse-grained soils is estimated from Table 5-2 using average SPT N60 values.
For dense, saturated silty sands, the corrected SPT value NʹSM = 15 + 0.5(Nʹ – 15) per Eq. 5-6.

equations.description: Elastic settlement equation: s = q0·B·µ0·µ1/Es, where µ0 and µ1 are influence factors for embedment and geometry/Poisson's ratio respectively.
Corrected SPT value for dense, saturated silty sands: NʹSM = 15 + 0.5(Nʹ – 15), where Nʹ is the average N60 value.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating elastic short-term settlement of coarse-grained soils by treating the soil as a linear elastic medium with known or estimated modulus Es.

sections.title: Schmertmann Method
sections.summary: Describes the Schmertmann Method for computing settlement of coarse-grained soils using a strain influence factor (Iz) distribution with depth, coupled with layer moduli derived from CPT or SPT. Presents equations for total settlement (Eq. 5-7), embedment correction C1 (Eq. 5-8), and time correction C2 (Eq. 5-9). Provides CPT-to-Es multipliers and SPT-based Es correlations via Table 5-3.
sections.body:
The Schmertmann Method is a common approach for the calculation of settlement for coarse-grained soils. This method uses typical patterns of vertical strain below a rigid foundation along with estimates of modulus based on either CPT or SPT. The variation of the strain influence factor (Iz) with depth is based on observations from model scale tests as well as numerical simulations. As shown in Figure 5-7, Iz increases with depth below the loaded area up to a peak value (Izp) and then decreases to zero at a depth of 2B for square footings and 4B for continuous footings. The magnitude of Izp is a function of the applied load and the effective vertical stress (σʹzp) at the depth of the peak influence factor.

The compressibility of the coarse-grained soil is incorporated through layer moduli estimated from CPT or SPT results. The soil profile immediately below the foundation is divided into layers with relatively constant cone tip bearing resistance, qc (or SPT blow count). Schmertmann et al. (1978) recommend that CPT qc values should be multiplied by 2.5 to obtain Es for axisymmetric (L=B) conditions. Similarly, CPT qc values should be multiplied by 3.5 to obtain Es for plane strain (L/B > 10) conditions.

Schmertmann (1970) provided multipliers to estimate qc from SPT blow count, N. Robertson and Cabal (2014) found a similar correlation between CPT and SPT. Table 5-3 combines the SPT-CPT correlation with the qc–Es correlation to provide approximate correlation between N60 and Es. The general values in Table 5-3 can be replaced by regional correlations that follow the principles provided in Schmertmann (1970) and Robertson et al. (1983).

The settlement (s) is then calculated for n layers as:

s = C1·C2·(q0 – σʹz0) · Σ[(Iz,i / Es,i)·Δzi]  (Eq. 5-7)

where:
C1 = coefficient to correct for the effects of embedment,
C2 = coefficient to correct for the effects of time,
q0 = applied foundation pressure,
σʹz0 = the existing vertical effective stress at the bottom of the foundation,
Iz,i = the average strain influence factor for the layer,
Es,i = the layer modulus, and
Δzi = the layer thickness.

The correction for foundation embedment is found from:

C1 = 1 – 0.5·(σʹz0 / (q0 – σʹz0)) ≥ 0.5  (Eq. 5-8)

The correction for time (t) in years after initial loading is:

C2 = 1 + 0.2·log(t / 0.1yr)  (Eq. 5-9)
key_points: The strain influence factor Iz peaks at depth then decreases to zero at 2B (square) or 4B (strip) below the foundation.
CPT qc is multiplied by 2.5 (axisymmetric, L=B) or 3.5 (plane strain, L/B>10) to obtain layer modulus Es.
Table 5-3 provides direct SPT N60-to-Es correlations combining the SPT-CPT and qc-Es relationships.
Total settlement is computed by Eq. 5-7, summing (Iz/Es)·Δz over all layers, scaled by C1 and C2.
C1 (Eq. 5-8) corrects for foundation embedment; minimum value is 0.5.
C2 (Eq. 5-9) corrects for time-dependent creep; increases logarithmically with years after loading.

equations.description: Schmertmann settlement equation: s = C1·C2·(q0–σʹz0)·Σ[(Iz,i/Es,i)·Δzi], summing strain influence factor over n layers with embedment and time corrections.
Embedment correction factor for Schmertmann Method: C1 = 1 – 0.5·(σʹz0/(q0–σʹz0)) ≥ 0.5.
Time correction factor for Schmertmann Method: C2 = 1 + 0.2·log(t/0.1yr), where t is time in years after initial loading.

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating short-term and time-adjusted settlement of coarse-grained soils using CPT or SPT data with the Schmertmann strain influence factor approach.

sections.title: Empirical Methods
sections.summary: Summarizes three empirical SPT-based settlement equations for coarse-grained soils (Terzaghi & Peck 1967, Meyerhof 1965/Duncan & Buchiagnani 1987, and Burland & Burbridge 1985/Terzaghi et al. 1996) presented in Table 5-4. These methods replace elastic modulus and influence factors with direct SPT blow count and foundation dimension correlations derived from plate load tests and observed foundation behavior.
sections.body: The difficulty of obtaining representative measures of compressibility or modulus for coarse-grained soils has led to the development of many different empirical methods. These methods are based on measurements and observations of load-settlement behavior from plate load tests as well as actual foundations. The underlying basis of these methods remains the elastic theory presented in Equation 5-5 but the soil modulus and influence factors are replaced with empirical correlations to SPT blow count and foundation dimensions. Three of the more popular relationships are provided in Table 5-4.
key_points: Empirical methods are rooted in elastic theory (Eq. 5-5) but replace Es and influence factors with SPT correlations.
Three methods are tabulated: Terzaghi & Peck (1967), Meyerhof/Duncan & Buchiagnani (1987), and Burland & Burbridge (1985).
Methods are calibrated from plate load tests and actual foundation case histories.
Burland & Burbridge method includes a shape factor Cs accounting for L/B ratio; approaches 1.56 for strip loads.
The Burland & Burbridge equation in Table 5-4 applies to ground surface loading on normally consolidated sand; corrections for embedment and overconsolidation require separate adjustments.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating short-term settlement of coarse-grained soils using SPT blow count and foundation geometry without requiring a separately determined elastic modulus.

sections.title: Accuracy and Reliability
sections.summary: Evaluates the accuracy and reliability of 12 SPT-based settlement methods and the Schmertmann CPT Method using 90+ case histories (Tan and Duncan 1991). Defines reliability as the percentage of cases where measured settlement was less than predicted. Shows via Figure 5-8 that the most accurate methods are only conservatively correct ~50% of the time, while more reliable methods (e.g., Terzaghi & Peck) tend to over-predict significantly.
sections.body:
Tan and Duncan (1991) provide a helpful perspective for assessing the usefulness of the various settlement methods for coarse-grained soils. They evaluated the accuracy and 'reliability' of 12 SPT-based methods and the Schmertmann CPT Method using more than 90 case histories. The most accurate methods will make a reliably conservative estimate of settlement (i.e., greater than or equal to the actual value) only about half of the time. Likewise, more reliable methods, such as Terzaghi and Peck (1967), tend to greatly over-predict settlement, which is well-documented. Figure 5-8 can be used to select an appropriate method for determining settlement for each project based on considerations of accuracy and reliability. In cases where more accuracy is required, one of the methods that plots to the lower left may be used. Where it is critical not to exceed the calculated settlement, a method with higher reliability can be used.

Note: In this context, reliability was defined as the percentage of cases where the measured settlement was less than the predicted settlement. Reliability is not used in a formal probabilistic sense in this case.
key_points: Tan and Duncan (1991) evaluated 13 settlement methods against 90+ case histories of coarse-grained soil foundations.
Reliability is defined as the percentage of cases where measured settlement was less than predicted (not a formal probabilistic measure).
The most accurate methods are conservatively correct only ~50% of the time.
More reliable methods (e.g., Terzaghi & Peck 1967) tend to substantially over-predict settlement.
Figure 5-8 provides a graphical comparison to guide method selection based on project accuracy vs. reliability requirements.
For accuracy-sensitive projects, methods plotting lower-left on Figure 5-8 are preferred; for conservative (no-exceed) requirements, use higher-reliability methods.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting among competing settlement calculation methods for coarse-grained soils based on the required balance of prediction accuracy versus conservative reliability.

sections.title: Long-Term Settlement of Coarse-Grained Soil
sections.summary: Covers creep (secondary compression) settlement of coarse-grained soils, estimated by multiplying short-term settlement by a time-dependent creep factor. Describes two approaches: the C2 factor from the Schmertmann Method (Eq. 5-9) and the stress-normalized creep factor Ct from Terzaghi et al. (1996) shown in Figure 5-9. Both share the same mathematical form; larger applied loads yield smaller Ct values since creep is a smaller fraction of total settlement.
sections.body: Creep or secondary compression of coarse-grained soil is sometimes considered by multiplying the calculated short-term settlement by a time-dependent influence factor. One suggested relationship is the creep factor (C2) included in the Schmertmann Method. This factor can also be applied to the results of other coarse-grained settlement methods. Terzaghi et al. (1996) suggest a similar approach to calculate a creep factor (Ct) which is related to the magnitude of the applied stress. The resulting values of Ct for their approach are summarized in Figure 5-9 where the applied stress (q0) is normalized by atmospheric pressure, Pa. For larger loads, this method predicts lower values of Ct because creep movements are a smaller proportion of the overall expected settlement. The creep factors for both methods have the same mathematical form. The total settlement at time (t) is found by multiplying the short-term settlement by the value of Ct.
key_points: Long-term creep settlement in coarse-grained soils is estimated by multiplying short-term settlement by a time-dependent creep factor.
The Schmertmann C2 factor (Eq. 5-9) can be applied to any short-term settlement method, not only Schmertmann.
Terzaghi et al. (1996) provide an alternative creep factor Ct normalized by atmospheric pressure (q0/Pa), shown in Figure 5-9.
Both creep factors share the same mathematical form; larger applied loads result in smaller Ct because creep is a smaller proportion of total settlement.
Total settlement at time t equals the short-term settlement multiplied by Ct.

equations.description: Time correction (creep) factor for Schmertmann Method: C2 = 1 + 0.2·log(t/0.1yr), where t is time in years after initial loading. Also referenced in Section 5-4.2 as applicable to other methods.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating long-term creep settlement of coarse-grained soils by applying a time-dependent multiplier to the calculated short-term settlement.

sections.title: Settlement of Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Top-level container section covering all aspects of settlement in fine-grained soils, including immediate settlement, primary consolidation (magnitude and time rate), and secondary compression. Organizes the four main subtopics: elastic/distortion immediate settlement, consolidation test-based primary settlement predictions, time-rate consolidation theory, and creep-based secondary compression.
key_points: Fine-grained soil settlement has three components: immediate, primary consolidation, and secondary compression.
Each component requires different analytical methods and soil parameters.
Accurate settlement prediction depends heavily on sample quality and reliable determination of preconsolidation stress.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever settlement analysis is required for fine-grained (cohesive) soil foundations.

sections.title: Immediate Settlement of Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Covers calculation of immediate (undrained) settlement in fine-grained soils via elastic compression or distortion without volume change. Describes use of Equation 5-5 and Figure 5-6 with Poisson's ratio of 0.5 for saturated clay, guidance on undrained modulus Eu from lab/field tests, empirical OCR-based correlations, and adjustment for partial yield when FS against bearing capacity is less than 3.
sections.body:
Immediate settlement of fine-grained soil is the result of one of two mechanisms: (1) "elastic" compression and volume change of the unsaturated soil or (2) distortion of saturated soil without volume change. Immediate settlement may be a significant proportion of settlement for unsaturated or heavily overconsolidated clay.

Similar to coarse-grained soil, immediate settlement of fine-grained soil can also be calculated using Equation 5-5 and the influence factors provided in Figure 5-6. For saturated clay, a Poisson's ratio of 0.5, which is the value assumed in the construction of the figure. In most cases, the undrained modulus (Eu) should be used. Values of Eu can be measured in laboratory or field tests, such as the pressuremeter. Caution should be used as laboratory tests may underestimate the magnitude of Eu. Similarly, field tests typically load the soil horizontally rather than vertically, which may lead to erroneous results. Empirical correlations, such as those in Figure 5-10, can be used for comparison or in place of test values when appropriate. OCR can be estimated from empirical correlations or measured using one-dimensional consolidation tests as described in Chapter 3.

If the factor of safety against bearing capacity failure is less than about 3 (see DM 7.2), then the immediate settlement should be modified to account for partial yield of the soil. D'Appolonia et al. (1971) can be used to determine the appropriate adjustment for this condition.
key_points: Immediate settlement in fine-grained soils results from elastic compression (unsaturated) or undrained distortion (saturated) without volume change.
Calculate using Eq. 5-5 with influence factors from Figure 5-6; use Poisson's ratio = 0.5 for saturated clay.
Undrained modulus Eu should be used; lab tests may underestimate Eu and field tests may give erroneous results due to horizontal loading direction.
Empirical correlations (Figure 5-10) relating Eu to OCR can be used when test values are unavailable or for comparison.
When FS against bearing capacity < ~3, modify immediate settlement for partial yield using D'Appolonia et al. (1971).
sections.applicability: Applies when computing immediate (undrained) settlement of fine-grained soil foundations, especially saturated or heavily overconsolidated clays.

sections.title: Primary Consolidation Settlement of Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Container section for primary consolidation settlement of fine-grained soils. Establishes the physical mechanism (pore pressure dissipation as water flows from saturated soil) and notes that accuracy depends on reliable preconsolidation stress determination and change in total stress. Overconsolidated soil settlements carry the largest percent error, tied to sample quality.
sections.body: Primary consolidation occurs as water flows from saturated soil and the excess pore water pressures caused by loading are able to dissipate. The magnitude of primary consolidation settlement can be predicted with reasonable accuracy when the soil's preconsolidation stress can be determined reliably and when the change in total stress can be accurately predicted. Settlement calculations involving recompression of overconsolidated soils tend to have the largest percent error. The amount of error for overconsolidated soils is related heavily to the quality of the samples used for consolidation tests, which affects the accuracy of the predicted recompression index and preconsolidation stress.
key_points: Primary consolidation occurs as excess pore water pressures dissipate following loading of saturated soil.
Prediction accuracy requires reliable preconsolidation stress and accurate change in total stress.
Overconsolidated soil settlements have the largest percent error, driven by sample quality affecting Cr and σ'p determination.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating the magnitude of primary consolidation settlement in saturated fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Use of Consolidation Test Results
sections.summary: Describes interpretation of one-dimensional consolidation tests for predicting swell, recompression, and virgin compression. Explains void ratio vs. log effective stress and vertical strain plots (Figure 5-11), defines modified compression index Cεc (Eq. 5-11) and modified recompression index Cεr (Eq. 5-10), and provides empirical correlations for Cc (Table 5-5, Figure 5-12). Cr is typically 5–10% of Cc.
sections.body:
One-dimensional consolidation tests are used to predict swell, recompression, and virgin compression of soils. Specific details about the testing process are described in further detail in Section 3-2.6. The results of consolidation tests are typically plotted in terms of void ratio vs. vertical effective stress or vertical strain vs. vertical effective stress. In either case, vertical effective stress (σʹz) will be plotted on a logarithmic scale.

Ideally, the soil behaves in the manner depicted in Figure 5-11 with log-linear segments describing the volume change or vertical strain that occurs as the vertical effective stress changes. The initial condition corresponds to initial vertical effective stress (σʹz0) and either the initial void ratio (e0) or to zero initial vertical strain, εz = 0. From the initial condition, the loading of overconsolidated soil results in relatively elastic recompression until the preconsolidation stress is reached. Any increase in σʹz that extends beyond σʹp results in plastic deformation or virgin compression. The slopes of these two lines are defined by the recompression index (Cr) and the compression index (Cc). A normally consolidated soil (σʹz0 = σʹp) will experience virgin compression due to any increase in σʹz.

Interpretation of consolidation tests in terms of vertical strain is often a more practical approach. This method emphasizes that prediction of strain is the intent of the calculations and will be used in much of the discussion in this chapter. The modified recompression index (Cεr) and the modified compression index (Cεc) are defined as Equations 5-10 and 5-11.

Methods for determining Cr, Cc, and σʹp from laboratory tests are illustrated in Figure 3-12. Many useful correlations have been developed between Cc and soil index properties. Table 5-5 provides a list of some of these correlations. Azzouz et al. (1976) found that correlations to e0 produced the most accurate prediction of Cc. Nine of the correlations are compared in Figure 5-12. Additional correlations can be found in Chapter 8.

The recompression index is typically 5 to 10% of the magnitude of Cc. Typical values for Cr fall in the range of 0.015 to 0.035 with nearly all results between 0.005 and 0.05 (Leonards 1976).
key_points: Consolidation test results are plotted as void ratio or vertical strain vs. log vertical effective stress, with log-linear segments for recompression and virgin compression.
Eq. 5-10 defines Cεr = Cr / (1 + e0); Eq. 5-11 defines Cεc = Cc / (1 + e0).
Cr is typically 5–10% of Cc; typical Cr range is 0.015–0.035 (nearly all results 0.005–0.05).
Table 5-5 lists empirical Cc correlations based on LL, e0, and wn; correlations to e0 are most accurate (Azzouz et al. 1976).
Normally consolidated soils (σ'z0 = σ'p) undergo virgin compression for any increase in vertical effective stress.

equations.description: Modified recompression index: Cεr = Cr / (1 + e0)
Modified compression index: Cεc = Cc / (1 + e0)

sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting consolidation test results and selecting compression indices for fine-grained soil settlement calculations.

sections.title: Magnitude of Primary Consolidation
sections.summary: Provides the three governing equations for primary consolidation settlement depending on consolidation state. Eq. 5-12 for normally consolidated soils, Eq. 5-13 for overconsolidated soils where final stress ≤ σ'p, and Eq. 5-14 for overconsolidated soils where final stress > σ'p (stress crosses preconsolidation). Includes layer subdivision guidance and worked example in Figure 5-13.
sections.body:
Primary consolidation settlement (sc) should be determined for each compressible layer. Thick layers should be divided into a series of sublayers (e.g., Figure 5-5b and c). For each layer, the appropriate equation for sc must be selected based on whether the soil is normally or overconsolidated and the relative magnitude of the change in vertical stress.

For normally consolidated soil (σʹz0 ≈ σʹp), calculate sc using Equation 5-12.

For overconsolidated soil layers in which the final stress is less than or equal to the preconsolidation stress (σʹz0 + ∆σz ≤ σʹp), calculate sc using Equation 5-13.

For overconsolidated soil layers in which the final stress is greater than the preconsolidation stress (σʹz0 + ∆σz > σʹp), calculate sc using Equation 5-14.

Equations 5-12 to 5-14 all follow a consistent pattern in which the compression or recompression index is multiplied by the logarithm of the change in stress to obtain the vertical strain. The strain is then multiplied by the layer thickness to obtain the change in thickness or expected settlement of the layer. In each of these equations, Cεc and Cεr can be replaced with Cc and Cr along with the initial void ratio, if desired, using Equations 5-10 and 5-11. Example calculations are shown in Figure 5-13.
key_points: Use Eq. 5-12 for normally consolidated soils (σ'z0 ≈ σ'p): sc = Cεc · H · log[(σ'z0 + Δσz) / σ'z0].
Use Eq. 5-13 for OC soils where final stress ≤ σ'p: sc = Cεr · H · log[(σ'z0 + Δσz) / σ'z0].
Use Eq. 5-14 for OC soils where final stress > σ'p: sc = H · [Cεr · log(σ'p / σ'z0) + Cεc · log((σ'z0 + Δσz) / σ'p)].
Thick layers must be subdivided into sublayers; compute sc for each sublayer at its midpoint stress.
Cεc and Cεr can be substituted with Cc and Cr using Eqs. 5-10 and 5-11 if void ratio basis is preferred.

equations.description: Primary consolidation settlement for normally consolidated soil: sc = Cεc · H · log[(σ'z0 + Δσz) / σ'z0]
Primary consolidation settlement for overconsolidated soil with final stress ≤ σ'p: sc = Cεr · H · log[(σ'z0 + Δσz) / σ'z0]
Primary consolidation settlement for overconsolidated soil with final stress > σ'p: sc = H · [Cεr · log(σ'p / σ'z0) + Cεc · log((σ'z0 + Δσz) / σ'p)]

sections.applicability: Applies when computing the magnitude of primary consolidation settlement for normally or overconsolidated fine-grained soil layers.

sections.title: Typical Construction Process
sections.summary: Illustrates how a sequence of typical construction activities (groundwater lowering, basement excavation, structural loading) generates cycles of consolidation settlement and swell in overconsolidated clay. Highlights that both settlement and heave can occur during different construction phases, and that actual magnitudes depend on construction rate and pore pressure dissipation rate.
sections.body: An example of the primary consolidation caused by changes in stress associated with typical construction processes is illustrated in Figure 5-14. In this example, the clay is overconsolidated by past loading. The construction process involves lowering the groundwater level, excavating for a basement level, and applying the structural load. Some aspects of construction will cause increases in effective stress and settlement. Other phases, such as excavation and groundwater rise, will result in swelling. As noted, the amount of settlement or swell experienced during the first phases of construction will depend on the rate of construction as well as the rate at which pore water pressures dissipate in the clay layer.
key_points: Groundwater lowering and structural loading increase effective stress and cause consolidation settlement.
Excavation and groundwater rebound reduce effective stress and cause swelling/heave.
The actual deformation during early construction phases depends on both construction rate and rate of pore pressure dissipation in the clay.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the sequence of vertical movements (settlement and heave) during a multi-phase construction project on overconsolidated clay.

sections.title: Corrections to the Magnitude of Consolidation Settlements
sections.summary: Describes when and how to apply a correction factor α to calculated primary consolidation settlements in overconsolidated clays when the load width is less than four times the clay layer thickness, deviating from one-dimensional consolidation assumptions. The correction factor α is obtained from Figure 5-15 per Leonards (1976).
sections.body: Settlement of overconsolidated clay layers may be overestimated using Equations 5-13 and 5-14 for loads of limited lateral extent. For cases where the width of the load is less than four times the thickness of the clay layer, conditions deviate significantly from one-dimensional consolidation. Leonards (1976) recommended that the corrected primary consolidation settlement can be found by multiplying the calculated value (Equation 5-13 or 5-14) by a correction factor, α. Values of α can be found using Figure 5-15.
key_points: Applies when load width < 4× clay layer thickness; one-dimensional assumption overestimates settlement.
Corrected settlement = calculated settlement × correction factor α (from Figure 5-15).
Based on Leonards (1976) recommendation for overconsolidated clays.
α accounts for lateral extent effects not captured in standard 1D consolidation equations.
figures: Figure 5-15 Correction Factor for Overconsolidated Clays and Loads of Limited Lateral Extent (after Leonards 1976)
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating consolidation settlements in overconsolidated clays under loads of limited lateral extent (width < 4× layer thickness).

sections.title: Time Rate of Primary Consolidation
sections.summary: Introduces the theory and methods for calculating the time rate of primary consolidation, including the time factor Tv for vertical drainage, average degree of consolidation Uz, and drainage path length Hdr. Covers both analytical and numerical approaches, single vs. double drainage, and the relationship between Tv and Uz via Figure 5-16.
sections.body:
The time rate of primary consolidation is considered for situations where predicted settlement exceeds tolerable values. In these cases, treatment of the foundation soil, such as acceleration of consolidation or placement of a surcharge to increase in preconsolidation stress, may be considered. Knowledge of the settlement rate or consolidation completed at a particular time is important for planning remedial measures for structures damaged by settlement.

Time rate calculations can be performed with greater accuracy and flexibility using numerical methods, such as the finite difference method. Various computer programs are available for this purpose. The analytical methods presented in this section are useful for understanding time rate of settlement concepts and checking the results of numerical methods.

The time rate of consolidation is typically assessed starting with one-dimensional theory applied to vertical drainage. The average degree of consolidation (Uz) is the average percentage of the excess pore pressure that has dissipated at a particular time (t) following the addition of a load. The amount of settlement experienced at the ground surface is typically assumed to be proportional to Uz. The value of Uz can be related to a time factor (T) for a given set of conditions. The time factor for vertical drainage (Tv) is calculated as:

Tv = cv·t / Hdr²   (5-15)

where:
cv = coefficient of consolidation for the soil layer in the vertical direction,
t = time after application of load, and
Hdr = drainage path length.

The relationship between Tv and Uz is provided in Figure 5-16.

Two conditions are typically considered for vertical drainage. Single (or one-way) drainage refers to conditions where water can flow one direction to leave the consolidating soil layer as shown in the inset to Figure 5-16. Double (or two-way) drainage occurs when pervious layers lie above and below the consolidating layer, and Hdr is half of the layer thickness (H) in this case.

The degree of compression (Uz) is the amount of pore water pressure that has been dissipated at a particular depth within the soil layer. The degree of compression will vary with time and depth within the consolidating layer as illustrated in Figure 5-17. It can be used to estimate the remaining excess pore pressures at any depth and time following application of a change in vertical stress. The upper half of this figure can be used for single drainage conditions.
key_points: Time rate of consolidation analysis is used when predicted settlements exceed tolerable limits, guiding remedial measures.
Time factor for vertical drainage: Tv = cv·t / Hdr²; relates time, soil stiffness, and drainage path length.
Average degree of consolidation Uz represents percentage of excess pore pressure dissipated; settlement is proportional to Uz.
Single drainage: Hdr = full layer thickness H; double drainage: Hdr = H/2.
Figure 5-16 gives Tv vs. Uz for instantaneous uniform loading; Figure 5-17 shows depth-varying degree of compression.
Numerical methods (e.g., finite difference) offer greater accuracy and flexibility than analytical solutions.

equations.description: Time factor for vertical drainage: Tv = cv·t / Hdr², where cv is the coefficient of consolidation, t is time after load application, and Hdr is the drainage path length.

figures: Figure 5-16 Degree of Consolidation for Instantaneous Uniform Loading and One-Dimensional Flow
Figure 5-17 Degree of Compression and Excess Pore Pressure (Contours Indicate the Time Factor)
sections.applicability: Applies when calculating the time rate of primary consolidation for foundation soils undergoing vertical drainage under applied loads.

sections.title: Effect of Initial Excess Pore Pressure Distribution
sections.summary: Discusses how the initial distribution of excess pore water pressure affects the rate of consolidation, particularly for single drainage conditions. Uniform distributions are covered by Figure 5-16; linearly varying distributions under double drainage are also covered, but complex cases require numerical solutions per Terzaghi et al. (1996).
sections.body:
The rate of consolidation can be affected by the initial distribution of excess pore water pressure, especially for single drainage conditions. The degrees of consolidation and compression predicted in Figure 5-16 and Figure 5-17 are appropriate for a uniform distribution of initial excess pore pressure, which is a reasonable assumption for relatively wide loads, regardless of the type of drainage.

Other scenarios, such as foundation loading and consolidation of hydraulic fill, can result in a distribution of initial excess pore pressure that is not constant with depth. Figure 5-16 is also appropriate for double drainage when the distribution of initial ux varies linearly. Solutions for single drainage and linearly varying distributions of initial ux can be found in Terzaghi et al. (1996). However, for these more complex loading conditions, numerical solutions are preferred.
key_points: Figures 5-16 and 5-17 assume uniform initial excess pore pressure distribution — valid for wide loads with any drainage type.
Foundation loading and hydraulic fill can produce non-uniform (e.g., linearly varying) initial excess pore pressure.
Figure 5-16 also applies to double drainage with linearly varying initial ux.
For single drainage with linearly varying ux, refer to Terzaghi et al. (1996); numerical methods preferred for complex cases.
figures: Figure 5-16 Degree of Consolidation for Instantaneous Uniform Loading and One-Dimensional Flow
Figure 5-17 Degree of Compression and Excess Pore Pressure (Contours Indicate the Time Factor)
sections.applicability: Applies when the initial distribution of excess pore water pressure is non-uniform with depth, particularly under single drainage conditions.

sections.title: Accuracy of Time Rate Predictions
sections.summary: Explains why field-observed consolidation rates are typically faster than 1D analytical predictions, covering three key factors: multi-dimensional drainage effects (Figure 5-18), presence of thin permeable seams reducing drainage path length, and anisotropy in hydraulic conductivity/coefficient of consolidation (Figure 5-19). Sample disturbance is also noted as a source of underestimation of cv.
sections.body:
The time rate of primary consolidation observed in field measurements is often faster than that predicted by the methods described in this section. This discrepancy is the result of a number of effects.

The theoretical conditions of one-dimensional consolidation and vertical drainage rarely mimic the in situ conditions. In most cases, loading and subsequent drainage is actually two or three-dimensional, which tends to increase the time rate of consolidation. As the width of the loaded area becomes small with respect to the thickness of the compressible layer, consolidation proceeds much more quickly. Figure 5-18 allows the time required to reach a degree of consolidation of either 50% or 90% to be corrected for two- and three-dimensional effects. The results are plotted for soil profiles with an impermeable layer below the compressible soil and for those with an underlying permeable layer. See Davis and Poulos (1972) for further details on these effects. Numerical methods can be used to account for some of these differences; however, many of the common programs used for consolidation calculations only consider one-dimensional flow.

Many clay soils contain thin seams of sand and silt, which have significantly higher permeability. These seams provide internal drainage boundaries, greatly reducing the maximum vertical drainage path length. For example, the presence of a single additional drainage layer can increase the time rate of settlement by a factor of four. In addition, soil deposits tend to have a higher horizontal hydraulic conductivity, which coupled with three-dimensional effects can increase the settlement rate. Figure 5-19 provides a simple means to account for effect of anisotropy in the coefficient of consolidation on the time required to reach 50% consolidation.

Finally, disturbance of soil samples tends to decrease the coefficient of consolidation measured in laboratory tests. Even high-quality samples and tests have some degree of disturbance, leading to lower cv and slower time rate of settlement predictions.
key_points: Field consolidation rates are typically faster than 1D analytical predictions due to several compounding factors.
2D/3D drainage effects accelerate consolidation; Figure 5-18 provides corrections for 50% and 90% consolidation times.
Thin permeable seams (sand/silt) reduce the effective drainage path; a single extra drainage layer can quadruple the settlement rate.
Higher horizontal hydraulic conductivity combined with 3D effects increases consolidation rate; Figure 5-19 corrects for anisotropy at 50% consolidation.
Sample disturbance reduces measured cv in lab tests, causing overly conservative (slow) time rate predictions.
Most common numerical programs consider only 1D flow and cannot fully capture these effects.
figures: Figure 5-18 Effect of Load Geometry on Time Rate of Consolidation (after Davis and Poulos 1972)
Figure 5-19 Effect of Anisotropy on Time Rate of Consolidation (after Davis and Poulos 1972)
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the reliability of 1D time rate of consolidation predictions and comparing them to field observations.

sections.title: Gradual Load Application
sections.summary: Addresses how the duration of the construction period (gradual load application) modifies the degree of consolidation vs. time factor relationship. Figure 5-20 (after Olson 1977) provides a graphical method to account for gradual loading in vertical drainage analyses, as opposed to the instantaneous loading assumed in standard 1D theory.
sections.body: The length of the construction period or the amount of time required to apply the load can also affect the time rate of primary consolidation. Gradual load application modifies the relationship between the degree of consolidation and the time factor. Figure 5-20 provides a method to account for gradual loading.
key_points: Standard 1D consolidation theory assumes instantaneous load application; gradual loading modifies the Uz vs. Tv relationship.
Figure 5-20 (after Olson 1977) provides a correction method for gradual load application under vertical drainage conditions.
Construction period duration must be considered when predicting time rate of settlement for embankments or staged fills.
figures: Figure 5-20 Degree of Consolidation for Gradual Load Application for Vertical Drainage (after Olson 1977)
sections.applicability: Applies when the load is applied gradually over a significant construction period rather than instantaneously.

sections.title: Coefficient of Consolidation
sections.summary: Overview of the three approaches for determining the coefficient of consolidation (cv): estimation from index properties (Chapter 8), laboratory measurement from incremental loading tests using Casagrande or Taylor methods, and back-calculation from field pore pressure dissipation measurements. This parent section introduces the two detailed subsections that follow.
sections.body: The coefficient of consolidation can be estimated based on index properties (see Chapter 8), calculated from volume change vs. time measurements in laboratory tests, or inferred from field measurements of pore pressure dissipation.
key_points: cv can be obtained via three methods: index property estimation, laboratory testing, or field pore pressure dissipation.
Laboratory and field methods are detailed in subsections 5-5.3.4.1 and 5-5.3.4.2 respectively.
Index property correlations for cv are covered in Chapter 8.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the coefficient of consolidation for use in time rate of consolidation calculations.

sections.title: Laboratory Measurement of Coefficient of Consolidation
sections.summary: Describes laboratory procedures for measuring the vertical (and directional) coefficient of consolidation cv from incrementally loaded 1D consolidation tests. Both the Casagrande and Taylor graphical methods are described (Figure 5-21). Also notes that constant rate of strain tests use a single equation for cv determination, and that shear strength test volume change data can be used.
sections.body: The vertical coefficient of consolidation, cv, is often found from data obtained using incrementally loaded one-dimensional consolidation tests on vertically oriented specimens. The coefficient of consolidation in other directions can be determined by trimming and mounting specimens in other orientations in the testing equipment. Regardless of the specimen orientation, the data is normally assessed using either the Casagrande or the Taylor method, which are described in Figure 5-21. Volume change measured during the consolidation phase of shear strength tests can also be used with these procedures. Other methods exist for determining cv from incrementally loaded consolidation tests, and a single equation can be used to determine cv from constant rate of strain consolidation tests.
key_points: cv is primarily determined from incrementally loaded 1D consolidation tests on vertically oriented specimens.
Specimens in other orientations yield directional coefficients of consolidation.
Casagrande and Taylor graphical methods are the standard approaches; both are illustrated in Figure 5-21.
Volume change data from shear strength test consolidation phases can also be used.
Constant rate of strain (CRS) consolidation tests use a single equation to determine cv.
figures: Figure 5-21 Determination of Coefficient of Consolidation from Laboratory Data (Note: the y-axis can also be plotted as volume or void ratio)
sections.applicability: Applies when measuring the coefficient of consolidation from laboratory consolidation or shear strength test data.

sections.title: Use of Field Measurements
sections.summary: Explains how in situ measurements of excess pore pressure dissipation can be used to back-calculate the coefficient of consolidation cv. The ratio ux/Δσv is plotted on Figure 5-17 at the appropriate normalized depth to read off the time factor, and cv is then calculated using Eq. 5-15. Figure 5-22 illustrates both lab and field cv determination.
sections.body:
Field observations of excess pore pressure dissipation with time can be used to measure the in situ coefficient of consolidation. At any given time after loading, the ratio of excess pore pressure to change in vertical stress (ux/∆σv) can be measured and plotted at the appropriate normalized depth on Figure 5-17. The corresponding time factor can be estimated from the contours, and cv can be calculated using Equation 5-15.

An example of both laboratory and field determination of cv is provided in Figure 5-22.
key_points: Field cv is back-calculated from measured excess pore pressure dissipation using Figure 5-17 and Eq. 5-15.
Plot ux/Δσv at normalized depth on Figure 5-17 to read time factor Tv, then solve Tv = cv·t/Hdr² for cv.
Field-derived cv values typically capture effects missed in lab tests (3D drainage, natural fabric, sample disturbance).
Figure 5-22 provides a worked example comparing lab and field cv determination.

equations.description: Time factor for vertical drainage: Tv = cv·t / Hdr²; used to back-calculate cv from field pore pressure dissipation data.

figures: Figure 5-17 Degree of Compression and Excess Pore Pressure (Contours Indicate the Time Factor)
Figure 5-22 Determination of cv from Lab and Field Data
sections.applicability: Applies when back-calculating the coefficient of consolidation from in situ pore pressure dissipation measurements after loading.

sections.title: Time Rate of Consolidation for Layered Profiles
sections.summary: Presents a step-by-step procedure for handling consolidating soil profiles with multiple layers having different cv values. The method converts the multi-layer system to an equivalent single layer by transforming each layer thickness proportional to the square root of the cv ratio. The equivalent single layer is then analyzed using standard methods such as Figure 5-16. Figure 5-23 provides a worked multi-layer example.
sections.body:
The consolidating soil may contain layers with varying values of cv. In this situation, the behavior of a layered system can be approximated by conversion to an equivalent single layer system using the following procedure:
