1. Select any layer (i) with properties cv,i and Hi.
2. Transform the thickness of every other layer with properties cv,n and Hn to an equivalent layer with the soil properties of layer i as follows:
   H'n = Hn · √(cv,i / cv,n)   (5-16)
3. Calculate the total thickness (H't) of the transformed system as:
   H't = Σ H'n   (5-17)
4. Treat the system as a single layer of thickness (H't) with coefficient of consolidation (cv,i).
5. Use the appropriate method, such as Figure 5-16, to determine the percent consolidation at various times.

The complexity introduced by multi-layer problems is well-suited to the use of numerical analysis for the calculation of time rate of settlement. An example of multi-layer time rate of consolidation calculation is provided in Figure 5-23.
key_points: Multi-layer profiles with varying cv values are converted to an equivalent single layer for analysis.
Each layer thickness is transformed: H'n = Hn·√(cv,i/cv,n), referencing properties of a selected reference layer i.
Total equivalent thickness H't = ΣH'n; the system is then analyzed as a single layer with cv,i.
Standard methods (e.g., Figure 5-16) apply to the transformed equivalent single layer.
Numerical analysis is preferred for multi-layer problems due to added complexity.
Figure 5-23 provides a worked example of the multi-layer consolidation calculation.

equations.description: Equivalent layer thickness transformation for multi-layer consolidation: H'n = Hn·√(cv,i / cv,n), converting layer n to equivalent thickness in terms of reference layer i properties.
Total transformed layer thickness: H't = Σ H'n, the sum of all equivalent layer thicknesses in the transformed single-layer system.

figures: Figure 5-16 Degree of Consolidation for Instantaneous Uniform Loading and One-Dimensional Flow
sections.applicability: Applies when the consolidating soil profile consists of multiple layers with differing coefficients of consolidation.

sections.title: Secondary Compression of Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Covers secondary compression settlement (ss) in fine-grained soils, which occurs due to particle rearrangement and creep under constant effective stress after primary consolidation. Presents the governing log-time equation, methods to estimate the secondary compression index Cα and modified index Cεα, the Cα/Cc ratio approach, and guidance on interpreting lab consolidation test data for secondary compression.
sections.body:
Secondary compression settlement (ss) occurs as soil particles rearrange and the soil structure creeps under constant vertical effective stress. For practical purposes, secondary compression can be assumed to occur after the end of primary consolidation and to follow a relatively linear trend with respect to time on a log scale such that:

s_s = C_εα * H_0 * log(t/t_p) = [C_α / (1 + e_0)] * H_0 * log(t/t_p)   (5-18)

where:
Cα = secondary compression index,
Cεα = modified secondary compression index,
e0 = initial void ratio,
t = time after loading,
tp = time required to finish primary consolidation, and
H0 = initial layer thickness.

Values of Cα or Cεα can be obtained from the results of a one-dimensional consolidation test that is allowed to creep for a significant length of time past the end of primary consolidation. The magnitude of Cα is stress dependent for a particular soil and should be determined at an effective stress similar to that expected in situ. For a variety of clays, silts, and organic soils, Mesri (1973) showed that Cεα is approximately related to the natural water content, wn, (in percent) by:

C_εα ≈ w_n × 10^(-4)   (5-5-19)

The secondary compression index is closely linked to the compression index, Cc. For this reason, an excellent method for estimating Cα is the use of the Cα / Cc ratio. Typical values of this ratio are found in Table 5-6. Recognizing that Cc is also stress-dependent, these ratios should be used with the slope of the laboratory virgin compression curve at the effective stress of interest (Mesri and Godlewski 1977, Mesri and Castro 1987) rather than the field corrected value typically used in consolidation calculations. An example of secondary compression settlement calculations is provided in Figure 5-24.

In many cases, one-dimensional consolidation tests are presented using the void ratio or vertical strain corresponding to the end of 24-hour load increments. Some amount of secondary compression will have occurred during this time period and is thus included in the laboratory consolidation curve. The engineer should be aware that consolidation settlements calculated with such data will account for some degree of secondary compression.

If secondary compression is expected to be important in the analysis, consolidation test results should be plotted based on the void ratio or vertical strain at the end of primary (EOP) consolidation for each load increment. Primary consolidation settlement calculated using the EOP consolidation curve can be added directly to estimates of secondary compression settlement.
key_points: Secondary compression occurs after primary consolidation ends, as soil creeps under constant effective stress; it follows a linear trend on a log-time scale.
The settlement equation uses either the secondary compression index Cα or the modified index Cεα, both obtainable from long-duration consolidation tests.
Cα is stress-dependent; it should be evaluated at the effective stress expected in situ, not at a generic value.
For clays, silts, and organic soils, Cεα ≈ wn × 10⁻⁴ (Mesri 1973), providing a quick estimate from natural water content.

The Cα/Cc ratio (Table 5-6) is a reliable estimation tool; values range from ~0.02 for granular soils to ~0.06 for peat, and should be applied to the lab virgin compression curve slope at the stress of interest.
Standard 24-hour-increment consolidation tests implicitly include some secondary compression; engineers must recognize this to avoid double-counting settlements.
For rigorous analyses, consolidation curves should be plotted at end-of-primary (EOP) consolidation so that primary and secondary settlements can be summed independently.

equations.description: Secondary compression settlement formula: ss = Cεα × H0 × log(t/tp) = [Cα/(1+e0)] × H0 × log(t/tp), relating settlement to the secondary compression indices, initial layer thickness, current time, and time to end of primary consolidation.
(force-injected from source text)

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating secondary compression (creep) settlement in fine-grained soils (clays, silts, organic soils, peat) after the end of primary consolidation.

sections.title: Differential and Tolerable Settlement
sections.summary: Top-level container section covering differential and tolerable settlement for structures. Addresses settlement patterns across a structure's footprint, quantification metrics (angular distortion and deflection ratio), tolerable limits by structure type, reduction strategies, and special considerations for mat foundations.
key_points: Differential settlement is typically more critical than total settlement for structural distress.
Angular distortion (δ/l) and deflection ratio (Δ/L) are the best indicators of structural distress from differential settlement.
Natural soil variability makes settlement calculations highly uncertain; approximate relationships are often sufficient.
Differential settlement for footings on sand is likely ≤75% of predicted total settlement; for clays it can approach total settlement.
sections.applicability: Applies to any structure where differential settlement must be evaluated alongside total settlement.

sections.title: Differential Settlement
sections.summary: Covers methods for characterizing differential settlement across a structure, including maximum differential settlement (δmax), rigid-body tilt (ω), angular distortion (δ/l), and deflection ratio (Δ/L). Distinguishes sagging (concave up) from hogging (concave down) and provides approximate relationships between differential and total settlement for sand and clay.
sections.body:
For important structures, settlement should be calculated for a number of points across the footprint of the structure in order to establish the expected settlement pattern. Figure 5-25 illustrates various types of settlement profiles.

Differences in settlement across a structure can be considered in multiple ways. The simplest is to consider the maximum difference in predicted settlement across the structure, which is often referred to as the differential settlement, δmax. However, it is often necessary and more informative to consider the effects of the size and flexibility of the structure when evaluating the impact of differential settlement. In some cases, a structure will tilt over an angle (ω) which causes difference in settlement between various points but does not necessarily cause structural distress.

Differential settlement that results in non-uniform deflection or non-uniform tilt causes bending and tensile strain in the structure. Differential movement that causes a concave upward shape is referred to as sagging while a concave downward shape is called hogging. This type of movement can be quantified by either the angular distortion or the deflection ratio. Angular distortion (δ / l) is the slope of the expected settlement profile or the ratio of the settlement between two points to the distance (l) separating the points. The deflection ratio (∆ / L) is the maximum expected deviation from uniform settlement divided by the overall length of the structure and is an approximate measure of the curvature caused by settlement. These two measures have been shown to provide the best indication of structural distress.

Natural variation in soil deposits causes settlement calculations to be highly uncertain. For this reason, it may be sufficient to use approximate relationships to estimate differential based on magnitude of total settlement. For example, Terzaghi et al. (1996) suggest that the differential settlement for footings on sand will likely be 75% or less of the predicted total settlement. For clays, the differential settlement can sometimes approach the magnitude of the total settlement.
key_points: Settlement should be calculated at multiple points across a structure's footprint to establish the full settlement pattern.
Rigid-body tilt (ω) can create settlement differences without causing structural distress.
Angular distortion δ/l = ratio of settlement between two points to the distance separating them; deflection ratio Δ/L = max deviation from uniform settlement divided by structure length.
Sagging = concave upward differential movement; hogging = concave downward differential movement.
For footings on sand, differential settlement is likely ≤75% of total settlement; for clays it can approach total settlement.
figures: Figure 5-25 Components of Settlement (after Duncan and Buchignani 1987, Ricceri and Soranzo 1985)
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating differential settlement patterns for any structure founded on soil.

sections.title: Tolerable Settlement
sections.summary: Container section for tolerable settlement criteria and reduction strategies. Covers the basis for acceptable settlement limits drawn from field observations, angular distortion criteria by structure type (Table 5-7), and Wroth and Burland's deflection ratio approach incorporating structural stiffness and L/H ratio (Figure 5-26).
key_points: Tolerable settlement guidance is empirically based on measured settlements and observed structural damage.
Differential settlement is the most important consideration for structural distress.
Structural design can reduce differential movement; many structures can tolerate large settlements and remain safe.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting tolerable settlement limits for structural design on any soil type.

sections.title: Criteria
sections.summary: Provides criteria for tolerable angular distortion and deflection ratios. Table 5-7 lists angular distortion limits (δ/l) for a wide range of structure types. Wroth and Burland (1974) deflection ratio criteria (Figure 5-26) explicitly account for structure L/H ratio, bending type, E/G ratio, and critical strain (εcrit = 0.075%) for a more rigorous assessment.
sections.body:
Most of the guidance regarding acceptable settlement is based on experience with measured settlement of real structures and observations of the associated damage. Wahls (1981) summarizes four important points regarding settlement: (1) settlement must be expected, (2) some form of differential settlement is the most important to consider for structural distress, (3) structural design can reduce the level of differential movement, and (4) many structures can tolerate large settlements and remain safe.

Table 5-7 provides guidance for the selection of tolerable angular distortion for various types of structures. In some cases, the limits that are provided include a margin of safety to reduce or prevent cracking or damage. Most of these guidelines ignore the size and stiffness of the structure, which control the magnitude of the strains in the structure.

Wroth and Burland (1974) proposed a deflection ratio criterion that allow the properties of the structure to be explicitly considered in terms of the controlling type of strain, the length to height ratio of the structure, and the structure's relative stiffness, E/G. Figure 5-26 plots these criteria for three different types of bending, assuming the critical strain for structural distress (εcrit) is 0.075%. Other values of E/G and εcrit can be considered using the equations provided on the figure.
key_points: Tolerable settlement criteria are empirically derived from real structure performance and damage observations (Wahls 1981).
Table 5-7 provides angular distortion limits (δ/l) ranging from 1/100 (slab-on-grade damage) to 1/2500 (load-bearing brick/concrete block walls, L/H ≤ 3).
Most tabulated limits ignore structure size and stiffness; the Wroth and Burland (1974) deflection ratio method explicitly incorporates L/H, E/G, and εcrit.
Default critical strain εcrit = 0.075% used in Figure 5-26; other values can be evaluated with equations on the figure.
Some limits in Table 5-7 include a safety factor to prevent cracking.
figures: Figure 5-26 Allowable Deflection Ratios Related to Structural Proportions (after Burland and Wroth 1974, Wahls 1981)
tables: Table 5-7 Angular Distortion Limits for Various Structures (after Skempton and MacDonald 1956, Polshin and Tokar 1957, Duncan and Buchignani 1987, and Day 1990)
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting specific angular distortion or deflection ratio limits for a given structure type and material finish.

sections.title: Reduction of Differential Settlement
sections.summary: Describes strategies to reduce differential settlement, noting that total settlement reduction (Section 5-7) is the primary approach. Discusses how load sequencing relative to consolidation rate can limit distress to sensitive finishes and machinery. Notes that flexible structures (e.g., light steel frames) may tolerate large settlements, shifting the design focus to utilities and equipment.
sections.body:
The reduction of total settlement (Section 5-7) is also the primary means of reducing differential movement. Settlement that occurs early in the construction process doesn't generally contribute to structural distress. The sequence and rate at which the load is applied can be compared to the expected rate of consolidation to estimate the total and differential settlement that will be experienced by different parts of the structure. If the consolidation rate is relatively fast, building finishes and other sensitive components may be installed after much of the total settlement has occurred and thus will experience less differential settlement than the superstructure. Estimates of this type of effect are heavily dependent on the rate of construction and consolidation and must be considered on a project-specific basis.

Some buildings, such as light steel frame structures, are very flexible and can tolerate large settlements. In this case, limitation of damage to utilities and machinery housed in the facility may control design.
key_points: Reducing total settlement (Section 5-7) is the primary means of reducing differential movement.
Settlement occurring before installation of sensitive finishes and components does not contribute to their distress.
Load application sequence vs. consolidation rate governs how much differential settlement affects various structural components.
For flexible structures (e.g., light steel frames), utility and machinery protection may govern design rather than structural distress.
Project-specific assessment of construction rate and consolidation rate is required for these estimates.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing construction sequences or selecting structural systems to minimize differential settlement distress.

sections.title: Differential Settlement of Mat Foundations
sections.summary: Addresses the particular challenges of predicting differential settlement for mat or raft foundations. Settlement calculations often assume uniform loading and stress distributions, but foundation rigidity and soil-structure interaction complicate this. Differential settlement predictions for mats are inherently less accurate than total or average settlement predictions.
sections.body: Settlement calculations for mat or raft foundations are often made based on changes in stress calculated assuming uniform loading. The rigidity of the foundation structure will affect the accuracy of this assumption and the distribution of settlement. The flexibility of the foundation and the soil structure interaction can be difficult to assess. Predictions of differential settlement are often less accurate than those for total or average settlement for these reasons, especially for mat foundations.
key_points: Mat foundation settlement calculations typically assume uniform loading for stress change estimation.
Foundation rigidity affects both the validity of the uniform loading assumption and the resulting settlement distribution.
Soil-structure interaction for mat foundations is difficult to assess accurately.
Differential settlement predictions for mats are inherently less accurate than total or average settlement predictions.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating differential settlement for mat or raft foundation systems.

sections.title: Methods of Controlling Settlement
sections.summary: Overview of methods to reduce, accelerate, or prevent excess settlement in compressible soils. References Table 5-9 which categorizes techniques by primary purpose: reducing soft soil, reinforcing soft soil, improving soft soil, accelerating consolidation, and reducing applied load. Points readers to FHWA Ground Modification Vol. 1 and 2 (2017) for in-depth treatment.
sections.body: Methods for reducing or accelerating settlement are summarized in Table 5-9. Further details for some of the basic methods are discussed in the following sections. For a more in-depth summary of ground modification techniques that can be used to remove settlement potential, reduce excess settlement, or accelerate settlement, see FHWA's Ground Modification Vol. 1 and 2 (2017).
key_points: Settlement control methods are grouped by primary purpose: reduce soft soil, reinforce soft soil, improve soft soil, accelerate consolidation, and reduce applied load.
Table 5-9 summarizes methods including removal/replacement, column-supported embankments, deep mixing, surcharge, PVDs, and compensated foundations.
FHWA Ground Modification Vol. 1 and 2 (2017) is the primary reference for in-depth guidance on ground modification techniques.
Mat stiffness factor (Km) from Table 5-8 guides flexible vs. rigid mat behavior before selecting a settlement control approach.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a strategy to reduce, prevent, or accelerate settlement under fills or structures on compressible soils.

sections.title: Removal or Displacement of Compressible Soils
sections.summary: Covers excavation and replacement as a method for eliminating settlement when compressible strata are shallow and thin. Discusses removal of organic soils and topsoil, partial displacement using fill weight assisted by jetting or blasting, and cautions against using partial displacement in fibrous organic soils due to risk of trapped pockets and differential settlement.
sections.body:
Excavation and replacement is a simple method of reducing or eliminating settlement for cases where the compressible stratum is shallow and relatively thin. This method is particularly useful for sites where extensive earthwork is already required.

Surficial soils with low shear strength and high compressibility, such as organic soils, should be removed and replaced with engineered fill. The suitability of deeper soils to support the planned fill or structure will depend on the shear strength and compressibility of the underlying soils as judged by an appropriate subsurface exploration. A common example of removal and replacement is the removal of topsoil which occurs prior to the placement of most fills.

In some cases, partial excavation of very soft foundation soils can be accompanied by displacement caused by the weight of the new fill. The boundary between the new fill and the displaced soil should be kept as vertical as possible. This method is most applicable to the displacement of peat and muck deposits and has been used successfully for soft soils up to 65 feet deep. Jetting and blasting methods can be used in the fill and foundation to facilitate displacement of the soft soil. Caution should be used with partial displacement in fibrous organic soils, as these materials tend to resist displacement, which can result in trapped pockets and differential settlement.
key_points: Best suited for shallow, thin compressible strata; especially effective where extensive earthwork is already planned.
Organic soils and other low-strength, high-compressibility surficial materials should be removed and replaced with engineered fill.
Partial displacement using fill weight has been successful in peat and muck up to 65 feet deep; jetting or blasting can assist displacement.
Avoid partial displacement in fibrous organic soils — resistance to displacement can create trapped pockets causing differential settlement.
Boundary between new fill and displaced soil should be kept as vertical as possible.
sections.applicability: Applies when compressible strata are shallow and relatively thin, or when organic/muck deposits can be displaced by fill weight.

sections.title: Balancing Load by Excavation
sections.summary: Describes the balanced (compensated/floating) foundation approach where permanent excavation offsets structural load, limiting net stress increase on compressible soils. Explains effects of dewatering on heave and recompression, how to compute net vertical stress (q0-net) using stress reduction (σz-red), and notes that settlement predictions follow Sections 5-3 to 5-5.
sections.body:
The balanced load approach (a.k.a. compensated foundation or floating foundation) can sometimes be used to support heavy structures over compressible strata. In this approach, the weight of the structure is balanced, completely or partially, by soil that is permanently excavated from the building footprint. The construction of a permanent basement level is required to create stress relief. This method works particularly well for situations where a stronger surface layer overlies a compressible stratum.

Excavation for the structure results in vertical stress relief and some amount of swelling or heave. If the weight of the structure is equal to or less than the weight of the excavated material, the total settlement experienced by the structure will be the result of recompression of the compressible strata. The magnitude of swelling and subsequent recompression will depend on construction and site factors, such as the amount of time between excavation and loading, the construction sequence, and the subsurface drainage conditions.

Dewatering may be required to facilitate the construction of a balanced foundation. If the groundwater is significantly lowered, the amount of heave and subsequent recompression will be reduced because of negative excess pore pressures in the soil.

Settlement for balanced foundations can be predicted using the methods in Sections 5-3 to 5-5. The net vertical stress (q0-net) is found by subtracting the vertical stress reduction (σz-red) from the building load, q0. The final groundwater conditions affect the value of σz-red. For cases where the groundwater is not lowered or is allowed to return to its initial condition following construction, σz-red is equal to the total vertical stress at the foundation level prior to construction. If the groundwater is lowered permanently below the foundation level, σz-red is equal to the effective vertical stress at the foundation level prior to construction.
key_points: Permanent basement excavation offsets structural weight, reducing net stress on compressible soils (compensated/floating foundation).
Works best when a stronger surface layer overlies a compressible stratum.
If structure weight ≤ excavated soil weight, settlement is only due to recompression, not virgin consolidation.
Dewatering reduces heave and recompression by generating negative excess pore pressures.
σz-red equals total vertical stress (if groundwater returns to original level) or effective vertical stress (if permanently lowered) at foundation level.
Settlement predictions use standard methods from Sections 5-3 to 5-5 applied to the net vertical stress.
sections.applicability: Applies when supporting heavy structures over compressible strata where permanent basement excavation can offset the structural load.

sections.title: Preconsolidation by Surcharge
sections.summary: Explains use of surcharge loading to induce primary consolidation and secondary compression before construction, with governing equations (Eq. 5-20 and 5-21) for the required degree of consolidation under the surcharge. Covers limitations including time, cost, and potential shear failure at surcharge edges. References Figures 5-27 and 5-28 for graphical solutions and worked examples.
sections.body:
A surcharge causes some or all of the consolidation to occur prior to construction. This method works well for fill beneath paved areas, for large floor loadings, and for structures with relatively light column loads. For heavier structures, improvement by surcharging may not be sufficient to provide adequate bearing resistance. In this case, a portion of the surficial layer of the compressible soil may need to be replaced with a more rigid compacted fill or reinforced fill.

A portion of the predicted consolidation and secondary compression can be removed by surcharging as illustrated in Figure 5-27. The calculations in this figure assume that the time rate of consolidation is the same under both the surcharge load and the final load. This should be approximately true provided the coefficient of consolidation is not significantly different under the two loading conditions. In order to eliminate the settlement due to primary consolidation under the final load, the degree of consolidation required under the surcharge (U+fs) is:

(Eq. 5-20)

where: qf = final applied load, qs = additional surcharge load, and σ′z0 = initial vertical effective stress at midpoint of the consolidating layer.

If some amount of secondary compression must also be removed by surcharging, the required degree of consolidation becomes:

(Eq. 5-21)

where: qf = final applied load, qs = additional surcharge load, σ′z0 = initial vertical effective stress at midpoint of the consolidating layer, Cα/Cc = ratio of secondary to primary compression indices, tp = time required for primary consolidation, and t = time after loading for which secondary compression is considered.

An example of the calculations for the surcharge approach is provided in Figure 5-28. The major limitations of the surcharge method are time and cost. The time required for consolidation to occur may not fit within the construction schedule. Use of vertical drains as described in the following section can alleviate this difficulty. In soft soils, shear failure can be induced at the edge of the surcharge. This should be considered using slope stability methods (Chapter 7) or bearing capacity theory (DM 7.2).
key_points: Surcharge loading induces primary consolidation and secondary compression before construction, reducing post-construction settlement.
Eq. 5-20 gives required degree of consolidation under surcharge to eliminate primary consolidation settlement under the final load.
Eq. 5-21 extends Eq. 5-20 to also account for removal of secondary compression, incorporating the Cα/Cc ratio.
Assumes coefficient of consolidation is similar under surcharge and final load conditions.
Major limitations: time required for consolidation may not fit construction schedule; cost of surcharge material.
Shear failure at surcharge edges in soft soils must be evaluated via slope stability (Chapter 7) or bearing capacity methods.
Vertical drains (Section 5-7.4) can be combined with surcharge to overcome the time limitation.

equations.description: Required degree of consolidation under surcharge (U+fs) to eliminate primary consolidation settlement under the final load, as a function of final load (qf), additional surcharge (qs), and initial vertical effective stress (σ′z0).

Required degree of consolidation under surcharge when secondary compression must also be removed, incorporating the ratio of secondary to primary compression indices (Cα/Cc), time for primary consolidation (tp), and time after loading (t).

sections.applicability: Applies when pre-construction surcharge loading is used to induce consolidation settlement before final structural loads are applied, particularly for fills, paved areas, or lightly loaded structures.

sections.title: Vertical Drains
sections.summary: Details the theory and design of vertical drains (especially PVDs) to accelerate consolidation by shortening drainage paths and exploiting horizontal hydraulic conductivity. Presents equations for radial time factor (Eq. 5-22), drain spacing factor (Eq. 5-23), equivalent PVD drain diameter (Eq. 5-24), smear factor (Eq. 5-25), and well resistance factor (Eq. 5-26), with references to design charts in Figures 5-29 through 5-32.
sections.body:
Vertical drains are constructed or inserted vertically through compressible soil layers. The drains intercept horizontal water flow. The water is then transmitted to a drainage layer at the surface and/or to underlying coarse-grained soil, depending on the drainage conditions. The drains are typically installed in triangular or square patterns as shown in Figure 5-29 with spacing ranging from 3 to 6.5 feet. Drains typically shorten the maximum drainage path to 8 feet or less. While vertical drains were constructed mostly of sand prior to the 1980s, current practice is to use drains comprised of a plastic core encased in geotextile fabric, typically referred to as prefabricated vertical drains (PVD). For detailed information on PVD materials and drain construction practices, see FHWA (2017).

In addition to shortening the drainage path, vertical drains take advantage of the higher hydraulic conductivity and coefficient of consolidation often found in horizontal direction in many soils. While the vertical coefficient of consolidation can be measured in laboratory tests or estimated based on index tests (see Chapters 3 and 8), the horizontal coefficient of consolidation (ch) is rarely measured directly. More often, ch is assumed to be about 1.5 to 4 times higher than cv, depending on the amount of horizontal layering present. Higher ratios of ch to cv are encountered when layers of silt and sand are present. Asaoka (1978) presents a method for determining ch from field measurements on a test fill.

Many analytical and numerical methods have been proposed for radial drainage theory, most based on Barron (1948). The differences in the methods tend to have less effect on predictions of consolidation rate than the uncertainty and variability in ch. Using the calculation method presented by FHWA (2017), the time factor (Tr) for a desired degree of radial consolidation (Ur) is found by:

If smear and well resistance are ignored, Fs and Fr are set equal to zero.

where: n = ratio of dc to dw. The error in the approximation is less than 10% for n greater than 4 and less than 1% for n greater than 12.

Given the uncertainties with the measurement or estimation of soil properties, the effects of soil disturbance or smear around the drains and drain resistance are often ignored (FHWA 2017). Smear tends to be important mostly for drains in high plasticity clays or sensitive soils, or where ch has been directly and accurately measured. key_points: PVDs (plastic core with geotextile fabric) are the current standard, replacing sand drains; typical spacing is 3–6.5 ft, reducing max drainage path to ≤8 ft.
ch is typically assumed 1.5–4× cv; higher ratios occur when silt/sand interlayers are present.
Eq. 5-22 gives the radial time factor Tr as a function of desired consolidation degree and factors Fn, Fs, Fr.
Eq. 5-23 provides the drain spacing factor Fn; the approximation error is <1% for n > 12.

Well resistance factor (Eq. 5-26) accounts for limited discharge capacity of the drain itself.
Radial consolidation theory is based primarily on Barron (1948); variability in ch dominates prediction uncertainty.

equations.description: Radial time factor Tr for a desired degree of radial consolidation Ur, incorporating drain spacing factor Fn, smear factor Fs, and well resistance factor Fr.
Drain spacing factor Fn as a function of n (ratio of effective drainage diameter dc to drain diameter dw), with an approximation valid to <1% for n > 12.
Equivalent circular drain diameter dw for rectangular PVD cross-sections, where a and b are the PVD dimensions: dw = 2(a+b)/π.
Soil disturbance (smear) factor Fs, approximated as ln(s) × (kh/ks), where s is the ratio of disturbed zone diameter to drain diameter and kh/ks is the hydraulic conductivity ratio.
Well resistance factor Fr accounting for drain discharge capacity qw, as a function of depth z, maximum drainage path length Lm, and horizontal hydraulic conductivity kh.

sections.applicability: Applies when vertical drains are used to accelerate consolidation of compressible soils by shortening drainage paths and exploiting horizontal hydraulic conductivity.

sections.title: Combination of Vertical and Horizontal Drainage Effects
sections.summary: Presents the Carrillo (1942) method for combining radial (horizontal) and vertical drainage contributions to compute the total combined degree of consolidation (Uc). The governing equation (Eq. 5-27) shows that Uc is not simply additive but uses a multiplicative complement of the individual degrees of consolidation.
sections.body:
Prediction of the degree of consolidation from vertical drainage can be combined with the effects of horizontal drainage to vertical drains using the method proposed by Carrillo (1942). The combined degree of consolidation (Uc) in percent is:

(Eq. 5-27)

where: Ur = degree of consolidation for radial drainage, and Uz = degree of consolidation for vertical drainage.
key_points: Carrillo (1942) method combines radial and vertical drainage effects without simple addition.
Eq. 5-27: Uc = 100 − [(100 − Ur)(100 − Uz)/100], expressed as percent.
Both Ur (from radial drain theory) and Uz (from 1D consolidation theory) must be computed independently before combining.
Combined Uc is always greater than either component alone, reflecting parallel drainage paths.

equations.description: Combined degree of consolidation Uc (%) accounting for both radial drainage (Ur) and vertical drainage (Uz) using the Carrillo (1942) method.

sections.applicability: Applies when both vertical (1D) and radial (horizontal) drainage paths are active simultaneously, as occurs with vertical drains installed through a consolidating layer.

sections.title: Vertical Drain Design
sections.summary: Describes the design procedure for selecting drain type, spacing, and construction procedures based on available time, target consolidation degree, and soil properties. Uses Eq. 5-22 or Figures 5-30/5-31 to determine radial time factor Tr, then Eq. 5-28 to compute required effective drain diameter dc. Figure 5-32 provides a direct design chart for drain spacing selection.
sections.body:
Vertical drain design involves the selection of the appropriate drain type, drain spacing, and construction procedures based on the time available for consolidation, design degree of consolidation for that time period, and soil properties. The appropriate time factor for radial drainage (Tr) can be determined from Equation 5-22 or from Figure 5-30 or Figure 5-31. Figure 5-30 plots the relationship between Ur and Tr for a range of drain spacing for three smear conditions. Figure 5-31 provides solutions for gradual loading and radial drainage. From Tr and the time available for consolidation (t) the required effective drain diameter (dc) can be calculated as:

(Eq. 5-28)

where: ch = coefficient of consolidation in the horizontal direction.

An alternative approach is provided in the design chart in Figure 5-32. This chart allows the spacing to be selected directly based on the other properties and variables. Other drain design considerations include stability against foundation failure and provision of adequate flow in the surface drainage blanket. An example of vertical drain design is provided in Figure 5-33.
key_points: Design inputs: time available for consolidation, target degree of consolidation, and horizontal coefficient of consolidation ch.
Tr is determined from Eq. 5-22 or graphically from Figures 5-30 (smear conditions) or 5-31 (gradual loading).
Eq. 5-28: dc = √(ch × t / Tr) — converts time factor to required effective drain spacing diameter.
Figure 5-32 design chart allows direct selection of drain spacing from project variables.
Design must also address slope stability against foundation failure and surface drainage blanket capacity.
Figure 5-33 provides a worked design example.

equations.description: Radial time factor Tr used in vertical drain design to determine the required time factor for a target degree of radial consolidation (referenced from Section 5-7.4).
Required effective drain diameter dc calculated from the radial time factor Tr, available consolidation time t, and horizontal coefficient of consolidation ch: dc = √(ch × t / Tr).

sections.applicability: Applies when designing a vertical drain system, including selection of drain type, spacing, and construction approach based on consolidation time requirements.

sections.title: Vertical Drains with Surcharge
sections.summary: Discusses combining vertical drains with a surcharge load to simultaneously accelerate settlement rate and achieve greater final settlement, particularly useful in soils prone to significant secondary compression. References the surcharge consolidation framework from Figure 5-27 as directly applicable when vertical drains are also present.
sections.body: In some cases, a surcharge is used along with vertical drains to accelerate the rate of settlement and reach the final settlement more quickly. Surcharges are especially important for soil conditions in which a large amount of secondary compression is likely to occur. The method presented in Figure 5-27 can also be used with vertical drains.
key_points: Combining surcharge with PVDs accelerates both the rate and total magnitude of pre-construction settlement.
Especially beneficial when significant secondary compression is expected in the soil.
Figure 5-27 surcharge calculation method (Eq. 5-20, Eq. 5-21) applies directly when vertical drains are also used.
This combination is a common approach for highway embankments over soft cohesive soils.
sections.applicability: Applies when both vertical drains and a surcharge load are used together to accelerate consolidation, particularly in soils with significant secondary compression potential.

sections.title: Construction Control Requirements
sections.summary: Covers field instrumentation and quality assurance requirements for vertical drain construction. Specifies that settlement plates are sufficient for low-risk fills; piezometers are needed to track pore pressure dissipation in large embankments over soft soil; and inclinometers monitor horizontal deformation. References FHWA (2017) for specifications and installation guidance.
sections.body: Extensive discussion of specifications, quality assurance, site preparation, and installation procedures for vertical drains can be found in FHWA (2017). Field instrumentation should be installed to monitor performance of the drains, progress of consolidation, and horizontal deformations. The type of instrumentation required depends on the application. For cases where instability is not likely, such as a low height fill of large lateral extent, the primary purpose of instrumentation is to monitor progress of consolidation. Settlement plates are sufficient for this purpose. On the other hand, stability and pore pressure dissipation is a concern for the construction of large embankments over soft soil. Piezometers should be used to monitor the dissipation of excess pore pressure during consolidation. Inclinometers should be installed to monitor horizontal deformations in the foundation soil.
key_points: FHWA (2017) is the primary reference for specifications, QA, and installation procedures for vertical drains.
Instrumentation type depends on risk: settlement plates suffice for low fills; piezometers and inclinometers required for large embankments.
Piezometers monitor excess pore pressure dissipation — critical for confirming consolidation progress under large embankments.
Inclinometers detect lateral deformation in foundation soil, providing early warning of instability.
Settlement plates provide direct measurement of consolidation progress for low-risk applications.
sections.applicability: Applies during construction and post-construction monitoring of vertical drain systems, particularly for embankments over soft soils where stability is a concern.

sections.title: Volume Expansion
sections.summary: Top-level container section for volume expansion of soils. Covers the mechanics driving swell, effects of expansion on structures, methods for estimating heave and swell pressure (empirical and stress-strain-suction), and practical design approaches for foundations in expansive soils and rock.
key_points: Volume expansion is driven by unloading/effective stress reduction, chemical processes, mineralogy, frost action, and oxidation of pyrite or anhydrite.
Expansive soil behavior is a critical design concern for foundations, pavements, and excavations in arid and semi-arid climates.
Both empirical and stress-strain-suction methods exist to estimate heave and swell pressure, each with differing data requirements and accuracy.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever soil or rock volume expansion (swelling, frost heave) is a potential concern in foundation or pavement design.

sections.title: Mechanics of Volume Expansion
sections.summary: Describes the physical and chemical mechanisms that drive soil volume expansion. Key factors include effective stress reduction from unloading or rising groundwater, osmotic and water adsorption processes, clay mineralogy (especially montmorillonite and smectite), matric suction, pyrite/anhydrite oxidation in shales, and frost-related ice lens formation in silts and fine sands.
sections.body:
Positive volume change or volume expansion of soil is controlled by a variety of factors. For fine-grained soils, these factors include physical particle interactions, chemical interactions, mineralogy, soil fabric or structure, stress history, temperature, and pore water chemistry.

Unloading or reduction in effective stress is the most important physical process that causes swelling in non-frozen soils. This unloading can be the result of a decrease in the total stress, such as that caused by an excavation, or as the result of increased positive pore water pressure from a raised groundwater level.

Various theories have attempted to explain the chemical processes associated with swelling, including osmotic pressure theory and water adsorption theory (Mitchell 1993). These theories predict the swell pressure, which is the pressure exerted by the swelling soil on an unyielding boundary. While such theories have a limited degree of accuracy and are not typically useful for practical application, they provide insight into general trends in soil behavior. The osmotic pressure concept shows that pore water with low electrolyte concentration leads to higher swell pressures. Similarly, according to water adsorption theory, the specific surface area of the clay particles is the most important factor for determining the amount of water required for hydration. For this reason, clay minerals with very thin particles with high surface area, such as montmorillonite, smectite, and vermiculite, are the most susceptible to swelling. The liquid limit and clay fraction are indicators of the amount of these swelling clay minerals present in a soil (Terzaghi et al. 1996).

Soil and rock that has been consolidated to a relatively low void ratio is the most susceptible to swelling. Low void ratios are the result of either high normal stresses or high levels of matric suction (ψ) under unsaturated conditions. The deformation experienced during consolidation stores energy in the soil particles. In addition, the water content in these soils may be lower than that required to fully hydrate the clay particles. If either the normal stress or the suction is lowered, the clay will tend to swell to release the stored energy and to hydrate the clay minerals. Some clay minerals, such as kaolinite, exhibit swelling mostly at the low void ratio associated with heavy overconsolidation. Clays containing more active minerals, such as sodium montmorillonite, experience similar amounts of swell regardless of void ratio because the swelling behavior is dominated by hydration.

Clay shales and shales containing pyrite (iron sulfide) or anhydrite (calcium sulphate) are also susceptible to swelling when exposed to water and/or air. The oxidation and hydration of pyrite and anhydrite can cause a volumetric expansion of ten times the original volume.

Soils can also experience volume expansion caused by freezing and the formation of ice lenses within the soil. Silts, silty sands, and fine sands are particularly susceptible to frost-related swell. These soils have moderate hydraulic conductivity which allows water to flow easily and a small enough void space to permit a significant level of capillary rise. For design of foundations in frost-susceptible soils, see ASCE (2001).
key_points: Reduction in effective stress (from excavation or rising groundwater) is the most important physical driver of swelling in non-frozen soils.
Clay minerals with high specific surface area (montmorillonite, smectite, vermiculite) are most susceptible to swelling; liquid limit and clay fraction are key indicators.
Low void ratios from high normal stress or high matric suction store energy that drives swell when stress or suction is reduced.
Pyrite and anhydrite oxidation in clay shales can cause volumetric expansion up to 10 times the original volume.
Silts and fine sands are most susceptible to frost heave due to moderate hydraulic conductivity and significant capillary rise potential.
Pore water with low electrolyte concentration leads to higher swell pressures per osmotic pressure theory.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the root causes and susceptibility of fine-grained soils, shales, and frost-prone soils to volume expansion.

sections.title: Effects of Volume Expansion
sections.summary: Describes the structural consequences of soil volume expansion, including heave below excavations, reloading cancellation of heave, differential swell-shrink patterns in arid climates (hogging deformation), and the difficulty of predicting movements during sequential construction stages. Notes that soft clays swell immediately and over time as water content increases.
sections.body:
Below an excavation, the total vertical stress is reduced, which initially causes a reduction in pore water pressure. As the pore water pressures return to equilibrium, the effective stress on the soil reduces and the soil swells. In most cases, excavation is followed by the construction of a building and the application of a pressure (q0) that meets or exceeds the reduction in total stress. In this case, the heave caused by stress reduction will be cancelled out by reloading. Movements during these stages of construction are typically difficult to predict.

Negligible heave is observed for excavations in coarse-grained soils above the water table. Soft clays will experience immediate distortion-related swell that can be predicted using the method in Section 5-5.1. However, the required elastic modulus can be very difficult to predict. Over time, clay soils will experience an increase in water content and swell as a result of the change in effective stress.

In arid climates, changes in water content tend to vary depending on the location below a structure. The soil below the middle of the structure interacts less with the environment, and the water content in this zone tends to increase with time. This results in swell below the middle of the structure. Around the edges, the soil experiences more fluctuation in water content and can shrink, leading to perimeter settlement. The combination of these two mechanisms can result in the hogging shape of differential movement described earlier.
key_points: Reduction in total vertical stress below an excavation initially decreases pore water pressure; as pressures equilibrate, effective stress drops and soil swells.
Reloading by subsequent structure construction (applying pressure q0) can cancel excavation-induced heave, but movements during construction stages are difficult to predict.
Coarse-grained soils above the water table experience negligible heave; soft clays exhibit both immediate distortion-related swell and long-term swell with increasing water content.
In arid climates, differential swell (center uplift) combined with perimeter shrinkage produces a hogging differential movement pattern beneath structures.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing structural impacts of swelling soils beneath excavations and structures, particularly in arid climates or in clay-rich deposits.

sections.title: Estimates of Heave or Swell Pressure
sections.summary: Overview of methods for estimating one-dimensional heave and swell pressure, including empirical index-property approaches and more rigorous stress-strain-suction methods. Discusses the depth of influence for stress-change-driven swell versus suction-driven swell (typically 3–15 ft), and references ASTM D4546 for laboratory swell pressure measurement.
sections.body:
Many methods have been proposed to estimate one-dimensional heave (vertical movement) or swell pressure. Some of these methods are empirical, based mostly on index properties of the soil. Other methods use theory and oedometer testing to predict swelling caused by both changes in total stress and changes in suction.

Most methods predict a swell percentage or vertical strain of the soil, which must be multiplied by the thickness of soil that experiences swell. The thickness of soil that swells as a result of a change in total stress, such as an excavation, is related to the size of the excavation. This depth of influence can be estimated using the methods presented in Chapter 4. The thickness of soil that swells due to changes in suction is related to the depth of the groundwater table and the depth of seasonal water content fluctuations, which is commonly in the range of 3 to 15 feet depending on climate.

In some cases, it is helpful to consider the swell pressure that an expansive soil or rock can develop against an unyielding support or structure under a certain set of initial conditions. ASTM D4546 provides three different methods to measure the swell pressure in a one-dimensional consolidation apparatus. The swell pressure mobilized in situ is often less than that measured in the laboratory (Terzaghi et al. 1996).
key_points: Heave estimates require multiplying the predicted swell strain by the thickness of soil that will swell; this depth differs for stress-driven versus suction-driven swell.
Suction-driven swell depth is typically 3 to 15 feet depending on climate and seasonal groundwater fluctuations.
ASTM D4546 provides three laboratory methods to measure swell pressure using a one-dimensional consolidation apparatus.
In situ swell pressure is generally less than laboratory-measured swell pressure (Terzaghi et al. 1996).
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and applying methods to quantify heave or swell pressure for foundation or pavement design in expansive soils.

sections.title: Empirical Relationships
sections.summary: Summarizes empirical correlations for predicting 1D heave and swell pressure, catalogued in Table 5-10. Methods draw on Atterberg limits, clay fraction, unit weight, water content, specific gravity, and initial suction. Highlights the limitations: correlations are based on limited datasets, cannot account for initial soil conditions when only index properties are used, and cannot capture the effect of stress changes on swelling.
sections.body:
Some of the available empirical correlations related to swelling are summarized in Table 5-10. These methods are mostly based on the Atterberg limits, clay fraction, and initial soil state as described by unit weight and water content. A few of the correlations require the soil's specific gravity or initial matric suction.

Correlations, such as those listed in Table 5-10, are useful because of their simplicity and the ready availability of input information. However, the correlations are based on limited data sets and are most appropriate for application in similar soils. In addition, correlations that are only based on Atterberg limits and clay fraction will not be able to account for differences caused by initial soil conditions. None of the correlations presented in Table 5-10 is able to account for the contribution of change in stress to heave or the effects of total normal stress on swelling.
key_points: Table 5-10 lists over 20 empirical methods for predicting 1D heave and swell pressure, primarily using Atterberg limits, clay fraction, unit weight, and water content.
Empirical correlations are simple and use readily available data but are based on limited datasets and most reliable only for similar soils.
Index-property-only correlations cannot account for differences in initial soil conditions or the effect of stress changes on swelling.
No empirical correlation in Table 5-10 captures the contribution of total normal stress change to heave.
sections.applicability: Applies during preliminary design or screening when index property data is available but advanced laboratory testing has not been performed.

sections.title: Stress-Strain-Suction Relationships
sections.summary: Describes more rigorous one-dimensional swell prediction methods that account for both total stress changes and suction changes, requiring suction-controlled oedometer or coefficient of linear extensibility tests. Notes analogy to consolidation theory and discusses time-dependent secondary swelling. Despite theoretical soundness, these methods are often impractical due to uncertainty in initial moisture conditions and unavailability of advanced testing.
sections.body:
More rigorous predictions of one-dimensional swelling consider the vertical strain that results both from changes in total stress and from changes in suction. These methods require measurement of the soil's stress-strain relationship, often at different levels of controlled suction. Suction-controlled oedometer tests and coefficient of linear extensibility tests are two means to obtain this data.

A variety of methods have been developed to predict the swelling strain caused by changes in total stress and changes in suction (or water content). Terzaghi et al. (1996) describes how the swelling process can be described in a manner analogous to consolidation. Vanapalli and Lu (2012) summarize many different methods to account for the stress-strain-suction relationship in the calculation of vertical strain based on the results of one-dimensional swell pressure measurements, suction-controlled oedometer tests, and coefficient of linear extensibility tests. Some of the methods also require measurement of matric suction as a function of water content. Terzaghi et al. (1996) also emphasizes that the deterioration of the clay structure during swelling often leads to a significant amount of time-dependent secondary swelling.

While theoretically sound, predictions of swell based on stress-strain-suction relationships are usually impractical. The amount of swell predicted by these methods is heavily dependent on soil moisture conditions at the start of construction, which cannot be accurately predicted during the design phase. In addition, the advanced soil testing required to use these methods is typically unavailable.
key_points: Stress-strain-suction methods predict swell vertical strain from both total stress changes and suction changes, analogous to consolidation theory.
Required testing includes suction-controlled oedometer tests and coefficient of linear extensibility tests, which are often unavailable in practice.
Clay structure deterioration during swelling can produce significant time-dependent secondary swelling (Terzaghi et al. 1996).
Despite theoretical soundness, these methods are usually impractical because initial soil moisture conditions at start of construction cannot be reliably predicted.
sections.applicability: Applies in high-consequence or research-level projects where advanced laboratory swell testing and suction measurement are feasible.

sections.title: Design in Expansive Soils
sections.summary: Summarizes foundation and pavement design strategies for expansive soils and rock, as catalogued in Table 5-11. Approaches include soil alteration (lime/cement admixtures), wet compaction, void zones (waffle slabs), eliminating water content changes, capillary breaks, sealing compounds for shale, designing piers to resist uplift below the active zone, and balancing swell pressure with structural loads.
sections.body: In many cases, heave and swell pressure estimates are used mostly to make decisions regarding remedial treatment of expansive soils and rock because of the uncertainties inherent in these estimates. Design of structures and pavements focuses on efforts to eliminate or reduce the effects of shrink-swell behavior of expansive soils and rock that are deemed to be problematic. Table 5-11 summarizes common approaches to foundation design in expansive soil and rock.
key_points: Heave estimates are often used primarily for remediation decisions rather than direct design calculations, given inherent uncertainties.
Soil alteration with lime, cement, or kiln dust reduces clay hydration demand and increases bonding to resist swelling.
Wet compaction (degree of saturation >80–85%) reduces swell potential but lowers dry unit weight, shear strength, and stability.
Void zones (e.g., waffle slabs) allow soil to swell into free space before loading the structure.
Drilled piers extended below the active zone with a bond break along the shaft in the active zone are a common structural approach to resist swell uplift forces.
Balancing swell pressure with structural bearing loads is feasible only for heavier structures where bearing pressure meets or exceeds swell pressure.
sections.applicability: Applies during foundation and pavement design when expansive soils or rock are present and mitigation or accommodation strategies must be selected.

sections.title: Construction Practices in Expansive Soils
sections.summary: Covers construction and maintenance practices to mitigate swelling and shrinkage in expansive soils and rock. Topics include limiting atmospheric exposure, controlling water content, surface drainage, rock bolts, compaction strategies for high plasticity clays, and use of admixtures such as cement or lime to reduce swell potential.
sections.body:
Good construction and maintenance practices in expansive soils and rock are primarily related to limiting exposure to the atmosphere and changes in water content. For swelling caused mostly by a temporary reduction in vertical stress, swelling can be reduced by collecting and removing surface water, pumping down groundwater, and placing a concrete mudmat immediately after excavation. Inert shale should be protected from wetting both during construction and long-term through the elimination of underdrainage, use of impervious backfill, and placement of appropriate surface drainage features. Excavations in shale should not be completed to final grade until foundation concrete is ready for placement. Some level of temporary and permanent protection can be provided through asphaltic coatings.

Some structures extend below future surface water or the groundwater table. In this case, access to water is impossible to avoid. The methods described in Table 5-11 can be used to reduce or restrict swelling. Where rock is shallow, rock bolts can be used with appropriately reinforced slabs and foundations to resist swelling.

For buildings in semi-arid and arid climates, changes in suction within the soil are the major cause of shrinking and swelling. Efforts should be made to collect surface and rain water near structures to prevent wetting of the soils during wet periods. During dry periods, evaporation and transpiration remove water from soil and increase suction leading to shrinkage. These effects can be limited through the use of pavement and avoiding placement of vegetation around structures.

Engineered fill constructed from high plasticity clays will tend to shrink and swell in response to the climate. In addition to deformation, this volume change results in a time-dependent reduction in shear strength that must be accounted for in slope design. If possible, high plasticity clays should not be used for the portions of embankments exposed to fluctuation in water content. Swelling of high plasticity clay fill can be avoided by compaction at high water content (i.e., wet of the line of optimums). Fill compacted wet will have lower dry unit weight, lower shear strength, and higher compressibility. High plasticity clay can be placed wet for structural fill below lightly loaded buildings provided the lower bearing capacity is considered. Consistent relative compaction is important to avoid differential settlement. Admixtures, such as cement or lime, can also be mixed with high plasticity clay fill during construction to reduce swelling potential.
key_points: Limit atmospheric exposure and water content changes in expansive soils; use mudmats immediately after excavation to reduce stress-relief swelling.
Protect inert shale from wetting via impervious backfill, surface drainage, and asphaltic coatings; do not complete excavations to final grade until concrete is ready.
Rock bolts with reinforced slabs/foundations can resist swelling where shallow rock is present.
In semi-arid/arid climates, control suction changes by collecting surface water and avoiding vegetation near structures.
High plasticity clay fill should be compacted wet of the line of optimums to avoid swelling, accepting trade-offs in strength and compressibility.
Cement or lime admixtures can reduce swelling potential of high plasticity clay fill.
Consistent relative compaction in high plasticity clay fill is critical to prevent differential settlement.
sections.applicability: Applies during design and construction of structures on or in expansive soils and rock, particularly in climates prone to significant moisture variation.

sections.title: Hydrocompression
sections.summary: Introduces hydrocompression — the volume change (collapse settlement) of compacted soil upon wetting after construction. Particularly problematic in deep fills of sandy clays and clayey sands, this phenomenon can produce significant differential settlements, with net settlement in deep fill areas and potential net swelling elsewhere.
sections.body: Hydrocompression refers to the volume change of compacted soil when wetted following construction. This phenomenon is especially problematic in deep fills constructed from sandy clays and clayey sands (Brandon et al. 1990). Significant settlement can occur in the regions of deep fill while net swelling may result in areas of shallower fill.
key_points: Hydrocompression is collapse settlement that occurs when compacted soil is wetted after construction is complete.
Deep fills of sandy clays and clayey sands are especially susceptible to hydrocompression (Brandon et al. 1990).
Differential behavior can occur across a site: significant settlement in deep fill zones versus net swelling in shallower fill areas.
Hydrocompression is distinct from swelling; it results in volume decrease (compression) rather than volume increase upon wetting.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating post-construction settlement risk in compacted fills, especially deep fills of sandy clays and clayey sands that may be inundated or wetted after construction.

sections.title: Notation
sections.summary: Defines all symbols and abbreviations used throughout Chapter 5 on soil mechanics and settlement. Covers geotechnical parameters including consolidation indices, drain geometry, SPT values, stress terms, time factors, degree-of-consolidation variables, and settlement correction factors — essential for interpreting equations and procedures in the chapter.

key_points: Schmertmann method symbols: C1 (embedment correction), C2 (creep correction), Iz (strain influence factor), Izp (peak influence factor), σʹzp (effective stress at peak Iz depth).
Consolidation indices: Cc (compression index), Cr (recompression index), Cα (secondary compression), and their modified (strain-based) counterparts Cεc, Cεr, Cεα.
Drain geometry symbols: dc (effective drainage diameter), dw (equivalent drain diameter), n (spacing ratio), s (disturbed zone ratio), qw (discharge capacity), Lm (maximum flow path).
Radial drainage factors: Fn (drain spacing), Fr (well resistance), Fs (smear/soil disturbance), used in prefabricated vertical drain (PVD) consolidation analyses.
Degree-of-consolidation terms: Uc (combined), Ur (radial), Ūz (average vertical), Uz (compression), Us+f (post-surcharge).
Structural distortion metrics: δ/l (angular distortion), δmax (differential settlement), ∆/L (deflection ratio), ω (tilt angle), εcrit (critical strain for structural distress).
Stress notation distinguishes total (σz, ∆σz, σz-red) from effective (σʹz, σʹz0, σʹzp, σʹp) vertical stresses, and includes matric suction ψ for unsaturated soil applications.
